#4679. Why Curlews Are the New Canaries in the Coal Mine

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

One would have to be totally out of touch to think that the Earth's diverse ecosystems are healthy and thriving. Numerous habitats are in dire straits, and many nonhuman animal residents are trying to tell us we must act to save everyone.

Grassland animals can tell us what is happening if we would only listen to them, and in her new book titled The Grassland Queen: An Avian Love Story in the American Plains, naturalist, filmmaker, and author Priyanka Kumar does just that by focusing on the lives of long-billed curlews, "an elegant shorebird with a rounded body and an improbably elongated bill—a highly intelligent bird that mates for life." I think of these birds as the proverbial canary in the coal mine, telling us that things where they live aren't going well, and Kumar carefully explains why we must listen to what they are saying.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you write The Grassland Queen?

Priyanka Kumar: As a naturalist and educator at the University of New Mexico, it’s my passion to research birds in the context of their ecosystems. The Grassland Queen shows how a community of birds can grow close to a naturalist’s heart, like they are extended family. Over years of researching curlews in grasslands, I returned to my daily life and found myself wondering how my birds were faring in the blazing fields, with heat radiating from dirt and stone.

The long-billed curlew is admittedly a strange-looking bird, with an impossibly long bill, like a creature out of prehistoric times. Curlew parents are insanely devoted to keeping their chicks safe from predators such as ravens, coyotes, foxes, and Swainson’s hawk. A curlew father is a Shakespearean character, dithering one moment, dive-bombing the next—I saw twists and turns and surprising bursts of drama on my days of fieldwork.

MB: How does your book relate to your background and general areas of interest?

PK: My work as a naturalist is deeply informed by my Himalayan childhood and how I experienced and loved nature as a child. I first wrote about long-billed curlews and a dozen other species in my book, Conversations with Birds. I am grateful that the book continues to resonate with readers and inspires them to deepen their engagement with nature.

Over time, I kept coming back to curlews. I wanted to observe them deeply. Long-billed curlews form lifelong pair bonds; the male and female may winter in different coastal areas, but they miraculously return each summer to the same grassland, find one another, and attempt to raise a family. They’re such relatable birds.

PK: Our national grasslands are one of the country’s best-kept secrets—the wildlife is exquisite, from the pronghorns to the burrowing owls. Grasslands have been very generous to humans—more than half of the human diet comes from grasses and their seed heads such as wheat, rice, rye, and oats. It’s time to return the favor and care about how grasslands are changing.

Grassland birds are in trouble—they’re the fastest-declining group of birds in North America. The ecosystem that the curlews have relied on for so long—they coevolved here with bison—is being relentlessly fragmented by industrial agriculture and development. Even the grasslands that remain are sometimes too degraded to support birds. My narrative about the curlew's life also shows a wider community of underappreciated grassland animals.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider and what are some of your major messages?

PK: It’s a marvel that curlews eke out a living in North American grasslands, which can sometimes look so scorched and bleak. Parts of the Great Plains have been in a megadrought, which means fewer grasshoppers and beetles for curlew chicks. These chicks need to eat, grow, learn to fly, and migrate back to the wetlands—without their parents—over one fraught summer.

It’s critical to understand the bird communities that live in the American Plains and how global warming can unravel ecosystems. After oceans, grasslands are the largest ecosystem on Earth. I take readers into the heart of this unfolding drama so that we can understand what the birds themselves may be experiencing.

MB: What challenge did you face while writing the book?

PK: The hardest part of writing this book was leaving the grasslands and all those lovely birds behind. In one of the last chapters, when I’m in the grasslands, I’m in wildfire smoke. With all the climate stresses, this ecosystem is pretty vulnerable to overheating and out-of-control wildfires.

Eighty percent of American grasslands are private, and we have no concerted national strategy—though there’s broad consensus that we need one—to incentivize private landowners to become more bird-friendly, whether through rotational grazing or creating wild margins at the edges of agricultural fields.

MB: Are you hopeful that as people learn more about this and treat birds with more respect and compassion?

PK: Literature and storytelling catalyze us to empathize with the lives of others. I hope this book pulls readers out of their everyday lives, transports them, and makes them feel affection for long-billed curlews. I’ve felt a sustained love for these birds over more than two decades.

I created an impressionistic painting: If you look closely, you’ll see many dots, which are the field observations. But hopefully, when you step back, you get the sweep of the grand landscape and the dramas playing out among wildlife and between wildlife and humans. This book is about being fiercely present. Will we choose to be present for the birds and the degradation their ecosystems face? It is painful to be present, especially when you find yourself looking for curlews on a shooting range, but there’s also a great joy that sneaks up on you just when you’re about to give up.

In conversation with Priyanka Kumar, an award-winning author whose writing has appeared in The New York Times, The Washington Post, Los Angeles Review of Books, Orion, and Sierra. An internationally acclaimed naturalist and filmmaker, she has taught at the University of California, Santa Cruz, and the University of Southern California and serves on the Advisory Council of the Leopold Writing Program.

#4678. Drug-Resistant ‘Superbugs’ Linked to More Than 50,000 Deaths a Year, CDC Says

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

New data show a substantial nationwide increase in potentially deadly infections caused by drug-resistant pathogens.

The updated Antimicrobial Resistance (AR) Threats Report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) states that drug-resistant bacteria and fungi cause approximately 9.7 million infections in the United States each year. This is up from 2.8 million in a similar report from 2019.

The estimated deaths in the United States from these drug-resistant pathogens have also risen from 35,000 to 50,800.

The new report also noted that infections that commonly occur in people in the hospital account for more than 42,000 deaths and cost the U.S. healthcare system more than $12 billion.

These findings are based on 2023 data. Officials from the CDC said that the increase in drug-resistant infections from 2019 partially reflects a real rise in infections caused by certain resistant bacteria and fungi. However, they also noted that data sources and methodologies have changed, and direct comparisons between the two reports shouldn’t be made.

“These numbers are alarming by any measure but are particularly sobering when infectious diseases physicians connect real patients with these statistics in their everyday experience,” Wendy Armstrong, MD, President of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA), said in a statement.

The CDC report highlighted 19 drug-resistant pathogens responsible for the 9.7 million annual infections. Four of these pathogens are classified as urgent threats, 13 as serious threats, and 2 as concerning.

The CDC also maintains a watch list that currently includes six pathogens.

The four pathogens classified as urgent threats are:

William Schaffner, MD, a professor of the Division of Infectious Diseases at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, told Healthline that the reason for this increase in superbugs is, “Overuse of antibiotics; using them for too long or in circumstances where they do not offer a benefit.”

“An example of the latter is the antibiotic treatment of common viral respiratory infections — antibiotics have no effect on viral infections. The widespread use of antibiotics kills off those bacteria that are susceptible to antibiotics, but then can leave a few bacterial survivors that are resistant to the effect of the antibiotics, resulting in the spread of these resistant strains,” he said.

Monica Gandhi, MD, a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco, agreed and added, “This widespread use leads to selective drug pressure on the pathogen to evolve resistance to these antibiotics, making them harder to treat.”

“The risk to public health from these bugs is substantial. In fact, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates up to 5 million deaths from these bugs worldwide every year, making these a substantial public health threat,” said Gandhi.

Candida auris tops the list of urgent threats.

Cases have increased nearly tenfold since the first detection in hospitals 10 years ago. This includes a more than 50% jump between 2022 and 2023.

Candida auris is a fungus that is almost completely resistant to one class of antifungal medications. It has also shown emerging resistance to the other two classes.

This fungus is often found on people’s skin, spreads rapidly in healthcare settings like hospitals, and affects some of the most vulnerable individuals.

CRE is a family of multidrug-resistant bacterial pathogens. They have become increasingly difficult to treat and can share resistance with other bacteria.

These bacteria also pose a significant threat to people in hospitals, especially those with devices such as ventilators and catheters. A recent study found that CRE cases at U.S. hospitals increased by 18% between 2019 and 2023.

While those in hospitals are especially vulnerable to CRE, 67% of the cases in 2023 were in the community. However, some of these cases may have occurred in people with recent exposure to healthcare.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the bacterium that causes gonorrhea, which is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections.

The CDC report noted that only a few antibiotics can effectively treat this infection.

Without effective treatment, gonorrhea can lead to:

There are ways you can help prevent these superbugs:

“[One] way individuals can help prevent the evolution of these superbugs is to not ask for antibiotics from their providers or urgent care settings in the setting of a viral infection,” said Gandhi.

Experts and organizations like the CDC are working together to find ways to reduce the spread of these superbugs.

“Professional organizations and hospitals are educating their doctors and staff about the antibiotic resistance problem and have created reviews of practice patterns to encourage the appropriate use of antibiotics,” said Schaffner.

Gandhi added that organizations should institute procedures, such as “antimicrobial stewardship programs,” to ensure that providers do not prescribe antibiotics for non-bacterial infections and narrow antibiotics as soon as possible.

The Pioneering Antimicrobial Subscriptions to End Upsurging Resistance (PASTEUR) Act aims to revitalize antibiotic and antifungal development by changing the way the federal government pays for novel antimicrobials.

This act was reintroduced in Congress in February and is currently under review.

The focus on reducing the spread of superbugs and developing new antibiotics is important.

“You really cannot have all the benefits of modern medicine, even outside the realm of infectious diseases, without effective antibiotics. It all goes away,” Haley Ann Pritchard, MD, medical director of infection prevention and antimicrobial stewardship at Eskenazi Health Hospital, said in a statement.

#4676. Bear with multiple tapeworms sticking out of its butt wins award

Published Oct 28, 2026 1:17 PM EDT

As intestinal parasites go, tapeworms are the stuff of nightmares. Though they can grow over 80 feet long in extreme cases, they often measure less than one-inch-wide. The intestinal parasites feast on their hosts, sucking valuable nutrients from mammals.

And then there’s the havoc they wreak on bear butts. One bear spotted in southeastern Alaska’s Tongass National Forest this summer knows all about that. The unnamed bear was spotted with multiple long tape worms poking out of its butt as it walked along Anan Creek.

“Seeing bears with a tapeworm is not uncommon at Anan,” the Rangers write. “but seeing one bear with multiple long tapeworms … yikes!”

For its service as a host to these long worms, the Rangers awarded this bear the 2026 Host with the Most Award. It’s a reminder that nature can truly be gnarly.

The United States Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest are currently doling out the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Tongass National Forest.

The nation’s largest national forest, Tongass covers most of Southeast Alaska, including the capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 known bears feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears (Ursus americanus) and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Like their counterparts further to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return here every summer to eat salmon and teach their young how to fish and survive. And also like the bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear and explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.

#4675. Could Ultra-Processed Foods Rewire Children’s Brains?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina

Could foods children eat change their brains? Can repeated exposure to sugar and ultra-processed foods alter children’s developing reward circuits in ways resembling the effects of addictive drugs?

An October 2026 study in JAMA Network Open provides an opportunity to revisit pioneering experiments by Bart Hoebel, Nicole Avena, and colleagues.

First, the new study. Kathleen A. Page and other investigators at Keck USC studied 46 healthy-weight children, averaging 8.7 years old. She measured ultra-processed food consumption, examined brain responses to food cues using functional MRI, and followed changes in weight and body fat over one year. According to the CDC, ultra-processed foods (UPFs) are low in dietary fiber, energy-dense, and contain little or no whole foods. They also include high amounts of sweeteners, salt, and unhealthy fats.

Children consuming more ultra-processed foods showed greater activation of the dorsal striatum, a brain region involved in reinforcement learning, motivation, and habitual behavior. Greater activation was associated with subsequent increases in body mass index and adiposity. Proof of food addiction? Not yet.

Increased activation does not always mean pathological reward processing. But could repeated exposure to highly rewarding foods alter how developing brains learn what to seek and consume?

More than three decades ago, Bart Hoebel, Nicole Avena, and colleagues at Princeton investigated whether sugar could produce addiction-like responses in laboratory rats. The rats really liked sugar. No surprise. So do most people.

But repeated cycles of sugar access, bingeing, and deprivation produced something more interesting: escalating consumption, withdrawal-like responses, and neurochemical adaptations.

Sugar bingeing repeatedly stimulated dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens. Endogenous opioid systems were also involved. In one remarkable experiment, naloxone (Narcan) precipitated withdrawal-like signs in sugar-binging rats. Sugar isn’t an opioid. Yet opioid-related mechanisms help make sugar so appealing.

The Princeton experiments established that particular patterns of sugar exposure could produce addiction-like adaptations in animals. The USC study asked if children's habitual UPF diets induce differences in developing reward circuits.

I subsequently collaborated with Hoebel and Avena, whom I mentored at the University of Florida, to investigate the overlap between drug addiction and excessive eating.

In 2011, Avena and I published “Food and Addiction—Sugars, Fats and Hedonic Overeating.” With Hoebel and Miriam Bocarsly, we also examined overlapping diagnostic concepts involving substance abuse and overeating.

Our question was simple: Why do people continue eating when no longer hungry? Maybe people really like how the food makes them feel- “hedonic eating.”

Nicole Avena, PhD, Professor of Neuroscience at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai and author of Sugarless, continues investigating these relationships.

Dr. Avena recently talked to me about the scientific challenge in studying overeating. Said Avena, “Food engages the same reward circuitry that drugs do--that part isn't controversial anymore. What we're still working out is which foods, how much, and at what age repeated exposure starts to change how the brain responds."

That distinction matters. It seems most important when discussing children and their development of eating habits and preferences.

Avena adds, "Calling a food addictive doesn't mean it's the same as cocaine. It means some of the same brain mechanisms (reward, craving, loss of control) can show up with food, and that's worth taking seriously."

But the brain does not maintain an entirely separate reward system for every rewarding substance.

Paul Kenny's lab extended this research, demonstrating reward dysfunction, altered dopamine signaling, and compulsive-like eating in animals exposed to highly palatable diets.

Dopamine participates in motivation, learning, and reinforcement. Endogenous opioids contribute to reward and hedonic responses. Learned cues may provoke seeking long after physiological needs have been satisfied.

My interest began in the 1970s studying cigarette smoking-induced weight loss and then cessation-related gain. Then, in the early ‘80s, I studied patients using cocaine or amphetamines who said they lost weight because they simply forgot to eat. But during abstinence, appetite returned.

Drugs changed eating and appetite. Stopping drugs changes that back again with a vengeance.

With University of Florida colleagues, I summarized these relationships in 2011. Subsequent experimental research with Orsini, Avena, and colleagues examined increased food consumption and weight gain following chronic amphetamine exposure.

Clinical observations suggested overlapping mechanisms involving dopamine, withdrawal, reinforcement, and appetite regulation.

In 2007, Kelly Brownell and I co-chaired the Yale Conference on Food and Addiction, bringing together nearly 40 experts. Nora Volkow delivered the keynote address. Brownell and I subsequently edited Food and Addiction: A Comprehensive Handbook. Ashley Gearhardt and colleagues developed the Yale Food Addiction Scale, permitting researchers to measure addiction-like eating behaviors.

At the time, comparing food and addiction was controversial. The accepted view was that food was necessary for survival. Cocaine was not.

True. But that was never the scientific question.

Kevin Hall's randomized inpatient study demonstrated that adults consumed approximately 500 additional calories daily on an ultra-processed diet compared with a minimally processed diet.

Importantly, obesity is not synonymous with food addiction. Some obese people don’t demonstrate addictive eating. Others show addiction-like eating without obesity.

Epigenetics offers another possible connection with eating patterns. Repeated exposure to cocaine, opioids, and other addictive drugs can produce persistent epigenetic changes in gene expression within reward circuits.

Eric Nestler and colleagues showed that addictive drugs alter gene regulation in reward circuits without changing DNA sequences. Animal studies suggest highly palatable diets may produce similar adaptations. These epigenetic changes are important, suggesting that highly rewarding diets like drugs similarly influence gene regulation and neural plasticity.

But these changes are not necessarily permanent.

Could repeated exposure to particular foods create a biological memory that makes them more difficult to resist? Possibly

Ultra-processed foods account for two-thirds of the calories American children consume, according to CDC experts. These often combine refined carbohydrates, fats, flavors, and textures engineered for palatability.

The child’s developing brain learns through repeated experience, shaping learning, preferences, and habits.

Not all ultra-processed foods are equivalent. The important questions concern which foods, which children, which developmental periods, and which exposures produce persistent effects.

The October study is provocative but small. Dietary intake was estimated, neuroimaging occurred once, and confounding remains possible.

Though we are accumulating impressive MRI data, association is not causation.

The science has advanced beyond our original experiments. The fundamental question remains: When does hedonic or rewarding eating become compulsive eating?

We need studies examining genetic vulnerability, early stress, food insecurity, and specific combinations of sugar and fat.

The objective is not to diagnose eight-year-olds with food addiction.

The question is no longer if food engages the brain's reward circuitry. Of course it does.

The question is whether repeated exposure to particular foods during childhood produces lasting changes in motivation, habits, and vulnerability to compulsive eating.

And whether those changes can be prevented—or reversed.

Children cannot choose the food environment we have created for them. Adults can.

#4674. Volkswagen’s EV battery recall reaches over 85,000, with Audi now included

Volkswagen’s latest recall now extends to Audi, affecting nearly 13,000 Q4 E-Tron and Q4 Sportback E-Tron vehicles globally. And just like with the ID.4, owners are being told to limit charging to 80% of the battery’s capacity.

Earlier this month, Volkswagen issued a recall with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) impacting 22,524 ID.4 electric SUVs, model years 2023 to 2026.

Official information from the German Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA) revealed shortly after that several thousand more VW Group electric vehicles are affected worldwide.

In three separate recalls now under investigation by the KBA, 72,668 VW Group EVs were included worldwide, including 9,881 in Germany.

The recall affects certain batches of the ID. Buzz, ID.3, ID.4, and ID.7 models produced between 2022 and 2025, as well as Cupra Born models from 2022 to 2024.

On October 27, VW Group added another electric vehicle to the KBA recall database. The latest recall impacts 12,734 Audi Q4 E-Tron and Q4 Sportback E-Tron vehicles globally, including just one in Germany. In total, Volkswagen’s battery recall now affects 85,402 EVs globally.

In the letter sent to the NHTSA on October 23, Volkswagen Group of America said it was issuing a recall affecting 9,048 Audi Q4 E-Tron and Q4 Sportback E-Tron vehicles in the US model years 2024 to 2025.

The recall stems from the risk of the battery overheating and potentially causing a fire under certain conditions when charged to over 80% of its limit.

Volkswagen said in a safety recall report with the NHTSA that “certain charging profiles combined with a state of charge over 80% may trigger thermal propagation.”

While the root cause is unknown, Volkswagen urged owners to limit charging to 80%. Owners of affected vehicles received an email saying VW “intends to apply a temporary vehicle setting that limits charging to 80%,” unless they opted out by October 21.

The safety recall follows Audi’s Product Safety Committee being informed of battery thermal events involving other Volkswagen Group EVs that use the same batteries as the Audi Q4 E-Tron.

Following an internal investigation, Audi found the same battery and production characteristics as the impacted VW Group vehicles. Audi said the majority of these were produced for the North American market.

Audi is not aware of any claims, crashes, fires, injuries, or deaths associated with the Q4 E-Tron’s battery issue.

Owners in the US can take their vehicles to an authorized Audi dealer, where the dealer will run a diagnostic check on the battery. If needed, the dealer will impose a temporary state-of-charge limit to 80%.

Audi expects to mail out interim letters notifying owners of the safety risks on December 18, 2026. Additional letters will send additional letters once a remedy is available.

Owners can contact Audi’s customer service at 1-800-253-2834 with questions or concerns. Audi’s recall number is 93SK. You can also contact the NHTSA Hotline at 1-888-327-4236 or visit nhtsa.gov for more information. The NHTSA campaign number is 26V698.

#4673. Dog’s paw print found in a 3,700-year-old brick

Published Oct 28, 2026 2:00 PM EDT

Archaeological relics often leave a lot to the imagination. Corroded jewelry and the tattered remnants of ancient clothing only tell part of a much larger story, but sometimes an object offers up a bit more detail. Occasionally, an artifact such as a piece of pottery is so well-preserved that even its creator’s signature is still legible thousands of years later.

In Turkey, archaeologists recently excavated an unexpectedly pristine example of one Bronze Age artist’s proof-of-authenticity. However, this wasn’t the work of a revered local craftsman. The marking appears to be the pawprint of a dog waltzing through a local construction site.

Turkey’s Ministry of Culture and Tourism Mehmet Nuri Ersoy highlighted the discovery earlier this month on social media. Archaeologists led by Erkan Fidan of Bilecik Şeyh Edebali University discovered the memento about 100 miles south of Istanbul at a site known as Tavşanlı Höyük. Spanning nearly 100 acres, Tavşanlı Höyük is one of the region’s most extensive Bronze Age mounds, and contains remnants of local Anatolian communities dating as far back as 8,000 years.

Fidan’s team has spent over five years excavating sections of the mound. In 2021, the archaeologists began investigating architectural debris that is roughly 3,700 years old. The debris included sections of mudbrick wall that were common at the time, which were made from combining water, soil, and straw into sections and then drying in the sun. But as one batch of mudbrick lay in the heat, a rogue dog apparently traipsed across a brick and left behind a near perfect, four-toed indentation.

“In Tavşanlı Höyük…we reveal not only structures and artifacts, but also such small and unexpected traces of life,” Esroy said in his post translated from Turkish.

After nearly 4,000 years, it’s impossible to know if a dog made its way across the bricks while workers weren’t looking, or if a human assisted his furry friend in making his mark. Either way, laborers still included it in the structure’s wall rather than discard the decorated mudbrick.

Tragically, archaeologists have since determined that the building eventually burned down with two people still inside. That said, a lack of canine remains suggests the paw’s owner was long gone before the blaze.

#4672. Taking Fish Oil to Boost Brain Health? A 2-Year Study Questions the Benefits

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A clinical trial found that taking high dose omega-3 supplements for 2 years did not help memory or thinking skills in older adults at increased risk of Alzheimer’s.Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC led the study, which was published in eBioMedicine. Participants took either a daily high dose supplement of omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) or a placebo.Fish oil is one of the most familiar ways people get omega-3s. However, the supplement in this clinical trial wasn’t made from fish, Hussein Yassine, MD, director of the USC Center for Personalized Brain Health with Keck Medicine of USC and the study’s lead researcher, told Healthline. This article uses the broader term omega-3 supplements.The researchers found that taking supplements raised omega-3 levels in participants’ brains, yet it didn’t change their memory, thinking skills, or brain structure.Dung Trinh, MD, an internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and chief medical officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, California, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings challenge the common belief that omega-3 supplements, such as fish oil, can help prevent Alzheimer’s disease or improve memory.Millions of older adults take omega-3 supplements. In a 2017–2018 federal survey, 21.8% of U.S. adults age 60 and older reported taking an omega-3 fatty acid supplement in the past 30 days, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Getting omega-3s from food or supplements is important since the body cannot make them.

Keck Medicine researchers enrolled 365 adults who did not have dementia, and whose ages ranged from 55 to 80, with an average age of 66.

Subjects obtained little DHA from their diets and had at least one risk factor for dementia. Of the 365 people who enrolled, 225 completed the trial, according to the study. Nearly half (47%) carried APOE4.Participants took either 2,000 milligrams (mg) of DHA or a placebo every day. Neither participants nor researchers knew who received the supplement.

The supplement in the trial contained more than 90% DHA and about 1% EPA, Yassine said.

Researchers found that high dose omega-3 supplements raised DHA levels in the fluid around the brain and spinal cord by 17%.

Both groups in the trial scored about the same on memory and thinking tests. Brain structure appeared the same in both groups.

The supplement also raised omega-3 levels in the blood. Over two years, participants’ omega-3 index, a measure of EPA and DHA in red blood cells, rose from 4.9% to 11%.“That’s a massive increase, but that doesn’t translate into clinical outcomes,” Yassine said.DHA reached the brain equally well in people with and without the gene variant APOE4, which is linked to a higher risk of Alzheimer’s disease, according to the study.Earlier trials couldn’t tell whether DHA failed to reach the brain or reached it without helping, the study’s authors say. This trial answers that open question, since the DHA got there.“This tells us that just because a supplement reaches the brain doesn’t necessarily mean it will improve brain function or prevent cognitive decline,” Trinh said.

The lack of measurable change in memory and thinking may come down to how the body uses omega-3s, according to Yassine.He said it’s “really important to distinguish between omega-3 metabolism and omega-3 supplements.”A supplement can raise omega-3 levels, yet the body may still break them down before they reach the right places. Obesity, smoking, and a lack of exercise can all reduce how much omega-3 gets into the brain, he said.

Some fish and fish oil supplements may offer more than omega-3s. These sources may also include other nutrients such as lutein, vitamin E, and selenium, Yassine said.A supplement can raise the level, but if you don’t change the holistic program, just going and increasing the level by itself may not be sufficient,” he said.Researchers tend to fall into two camps on how to read the results, according to Yassine.

Some see the findings as evidence that supplements don’t work in isolation. Others argue the trial would need a longer follow-up or sicker participants to answer the question.Trinh pointed to the study’s length. “It’s also important to recognize that Alzheimer’s disease develops over decades, so a two-year study may not be long enough to determine whether DHA supplementation has any long-term preventive benefits,” he said.

Fish oil supplements contain two omega-3 fatty acids, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and DHA, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH).

Foods such as fish and flaxseed also contain omega-3s, according to the National Institutes of Health’s Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS).Research suggests omega-3s may help reduce inflammation, support heart health, and promote childhood growth and development.

Some observational studies link diets high in omega-3s with a lower risk of cognitive decline and dementia.

Researchers say omega-3s may help preserve cognition by supporting brain cells in continuing to function and maintain their membranes, according to the ODS.“Omega-3s are important for the brain, and we and many others have shown that having higher levels of omega-3s is associated with less Alzheimer’s pathology, better cognition, and many other protective outcomes,” Yassine said, in contrast to the trial findings.Trinh agreed. “DHA plays an essential role in maintaining healthy brain cells, and there is evidence that eating fish as part of a healthy dietary pattern may support long-term brain health,” he said.Research on omega-3s and brain health is ongoing, and there is insufficient evidence to draw firm conclusions about their effectiveness.

Some people may still benefit from a supplement, according to Yassine, including:

Some neurologists test omega-3 levels, though the test isn’t standard, Yassine said.People with nutritional deficiencies or certain genetic or metabolic traits may respond differently to omega-3 supplements, and researchers still need to learn who might benefit, Trinh said.

People who already take fish oil or other omega-3 supplements for other reasons, such as high triglycerides, should make those decisions with their healthcare professionals, he said.

Trinh said he tells his patients that “what is good for the heart is generally good for the brain.” He recommended the following healthy habits:

“Overall, this study reminds us that there is no magic pill for preventing Alzheimer’s disease and that maintaining brain health requires a much broader approach,” Trinh said.

#4671. Dems introduce new $15,000 EV tax credit bill that has no chance — and that’s a problem

Rep. Greg Landsman (D-OH) wants to bring back the federal EV tax credit and double it. His new bill, the “21st Century Vehicle Choice Act” (H.R. 10881), would offer up to $15,000 on a new electric vehicle and $8,000 on a used one, and it would make both credits permanent.

The problem is that the bill has virtually no chance of becoming law anytime soon. And if EV shoppers start holding out for it, it could end up hurting the market it’s trying to help.

Landsman introduced H.R. 10881 on October 22. It was referred to three House committees (Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Natural Resources), and as of today, it doesn’t have a single cosponsor.

The big change is to the new clean vehicle credit, Section 30D of the tax code. Under the Inflation Reduction Act, the $7,500 credit came in two $3,750 halves: one for meeting critical mineral sourcing requirements and one for battery components. Landsman’s bill doubles each half to $7,500, for a maximum of $15,000.

It also deletes the termination dates. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act killed the new and used EV credits for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, and the home charger credit after June 30, 2026. Striking those dates would revive all three credits with no expiration.

The bill doesn’t touch the rest of 30D. North American final assembly, the $55,000 MSRP cap on cars and $80,000 cap on SUVs, pickups, and vans, and the foreign entity of concern rules all stay. So the full $15,000 would only go to EVs that clear both sourcing tests, which has always been a short list.

The rest of the bill is reports. Commerce would deliver a “Vehicle Choice Report” on vehicle variety and ownership costs, and the Department of Energy would file five years of critical minerals reports.

The most interesting part is a DOE study of “gasoline super-users,” defined as the top 10% of light-duty vehicle owners by gas consumption. The study would map the regions where they’re concentrated and their 100 most-used routes, then track charger availability along those routes every year for five years. Coltura, which backs the bill, says the highest-mileage drivers spend over 10% of household income on fuel.

Republicans control both the House and the Senate, and they’re the ones who just repealed these credits. President Trump signed that repeal.

Even if Democrats flip the House and Senate in next week’s midterms, a bill restoring EV credits would still need to get through a veto. So realistically, nothing like this happens before 2029.

It’s also a rerun. Landsman introduced the exact same “21st Century Vehicle Choice Act” as H.R. 10046 on October 25, 2024, 11 days before that year’s election. It got zero cosponsors and died in committee. This version landed 12 days before the November 3 midterms.

This is where the bill can do real damage. EV buyers are extremely sensitive to tax credit timing, and the last year proved it.

When the credit was about to disappear, buyers rushed in, and Q3 2025 became the best quarter ever for US EV sales, with market share topping 10% for the first time. Then the floor dropped out. Hyundai’s Ioniq 5 sales fell 63% the month after the credit ended.

The market is only now crawling back. According to Cox Automotive, US EV sales hit 262,649 units in Q3 2026, up 6.1% from Q2 but still down 39.5% year-over-year, at a 6.4% share of new vehicle sales. Tesla’s Model Y and Model 3 still dominate, but Toyota, Rivian, and Hyundai are growing again.

That recovery is fragile. A headline promising “$15,000 off your next EV” is exactly what makes a shopper on the fence decide to wait a year or two.

And waiting gets you nothing. The new credits would only apply to vehicles placed in service after the bill is enacted, so there’s no retroactive payout for buying now. If you already claimed the credit once, you’d get $0 anyway.

Meanwhile, the deals on the lot are real. Automakers have been cutting prices to make up for the lost credit, like Hyundai, which cut the 2026 Ioniq 5 by nearly $10,000 on some trims.

At Electrek, our position has always been clear: we think EVs are a net positive and ICE vehicles have unpriced externalities. Therefore, we will take whatever we can get to encourage EV sales, but our preferred approach would be a carbon tax on ICE vehicles.

We’ve been clear that policy shapes this market. Killing the $7,500 credit is the main reason US EV sales collapsed. Consumers didn’t suddenly decide they hate EVs. So we’re all for bringing incentives back.

But this bill is messaging. It has zero cosponsors and no CBO score, and it dropped two weeks before an election, just like the identical version two years ago.

They should focus on rooftop and community solar tax credits and initiatives. With rising electric rates, helping people alleviate those would be vastly more popular than EV subsidies.

To be fair, some of it is smart. The lower income caps and the once-per-taxpayer limit go after the most common criticism of the old credit, that it subsidized wealthy households buying their second or third EV. And the “super-user” study is the best idea in the bill. Getting a high-mileage driver out of a gas pickup does far more for fuel costs and emissions than putting a low-mileage commuter in their second Tesla. If Democrats want to rebuild EV policy in 2029, that’s where they should start.

The problem is that people will hear the headline number. If you need a car now and an EV fits your life, buy it now and take the deals that are on the table. Don’t plan your purchase around a bill that has no path to passing for at least two years.

Will Democrats come back with a real, cosponsored EV plan before 2028? I don’t know, but I suspect that the US will continue to fall behind the rest of the world when it comes to EV adoption.

If you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero, with or without a tax credit. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4670. Touchscreen shirt shows photos, plays videos, and answers calls

Published Oct 28, 2026 3:04 PM EDT

Engineers and computer scientists have spent the better part of the past 15 years trying to integrate mobile phone technology into clothing. The closest example of these so-called “smart clothes” becoming a retail reality came in 2017, when blue jean behemoth Levi teamed up with Google to release its Jacquard trucker jacket. On the surface, it looked just like the iconic denim original, but its cuff had touch sensors and haptic feedback built in. By fiddling with those inputs, wearers could control aspects of their connected smartphone like pausing and and skipping forward music, receive vibration alters or even remotely snap a photo, all without ever having to stop and look down at the phone’s screen.

Jacquard was a technological leap, but its relatively simple input system meant its uses were incredibly barebones, andGoogle eventually shuttered Jacquard  in 2023. For smart clothes to  meaningfully “replace” a mobile phone, the clothes themselves would need to function as a screen. That challenge has proven far more daunting, but a team from National University of Singapore college of Design and Engineering believes it has taken significant steps forward with what it’s calling the world’s first touchscreen built into a garment. They managed to pull this off by engineering a flexible, wearable fiber made up of 54 electronic fibers that functions like a digital image pixel. That fiber can be weaved into clothing to create a space on the user’s forearm that looks and functions like a smartphone screen.

In testing, researchers wearing the touchscreen shirt connected it to their phones, and used it to scroll through photos. This shirt/screen hybrid also played videos at 30 frames per second, which isn’t exactly right for top-tier viewing, but is certainly passable. The team were also able to tap on the touchscreen shirt to check notifications and use its Bluetooth connection to issue voice commands. It can even run the calculator app. Talk about some back-of-the-hand math.

The touchscreen shirt isn’t ready for mainstream use yet, but it offers one of the clearest templates yet for how smart clothes could pull increasingly distracted brains away from smartphone screens.

The team published their findings recently in the journal Nature

“What made this possible was our ability to construct the GUI system from electronic building blocks in fiber form—similar to traditional yarn, but with the sophisticated electronic functionality built directly into the fibers,” National University of Singapore college of Design and Engineering assistant professor Tural Khudiyev said in a statement.

Turning fiber into a relatable digital input isn’t easy. The team set out to develop a method for creating connection points along tiny insulated wires right where each accompanying microchip would need them. They used a laser light to precisely guide molten solder, a process used in circuit board manufacturing that ensures melted metal only bonds at precise points along the wire. The resulting strip of LEDs was then drawn into a multilayer thread one one millimeter thick, which is thinner than a credit card. In total, the team says it integrated more than 5,000 chips through more than 20,0000 electrical components into the fabric.

“A fiber has a one-dimensional, axially symmetric geometry, which makes it difficult to build complex circuitry using approaches developed for conventional two-dimensional electronics,” Khudiyev added. “We overcame this limitation through a new interconnection architecture, which enables thousands of microelectronic devices to be integrated and interconnected along a fiber.”

Once fully woven into a garment, the smart fibers form a 6.6 by 4.3 inch display screen. The screen itself can register several touches at once and supports 8-bit color depth, which gives it a kind of a shimmering visual profile somewhat reminiscent of late 1980s and early 1990s arcade video games. The entire is woven into the garment’s inner forearm.

In terms of functionality, the touchscreen clothing is admittedly closer to early smartphones than a newer device like the iPhone Duo. Images provided by the researchers show the sleeve displaying photos of tigers, parrots and classical marble statues, all with a fuzzy but passable resolution. In the footage shared in the study,  the videos seem to play smoothly at 30 frames per second, but only without sound. Syncing the audio to the video drops that to 25 frames per second, which makes playback noticeably choppier. It’s also not entirely clear how the garment is powered or how long it can run before it needs a charge.

Despite those limitations, the sleeve still mostly works as a mobile device. Just as importantly though, it also works as a shirt. Wearing smart clothing shouldn’t feel like being tightly wrapped in ethernet cables. In this case, the team says its woven display is as breathable as denim and heavy cotton. To test the touchscreen’s durability, they burnt the barricade 1,000 times and ran it through washing machines for 50 cycles. Even after that abuse, the display and touch sensors worked nearly as well as they did before.

Smart clothing supporters say more advanced iterations of devices like these could help more accurately monitor a user’s health data and display that back to them in a quickly accessible and feasible form factor. Khudiyev argues this form factor, especially when merged with AI systems, “could enable personalized health monitoring, feedback and assistance.”

While there’s also a growing push to divert attention away from mobile phone screens,this device only partially addresses that problem. Some functions like receiving messages can be performed on the smart fabric, but viewing photos and and video on it essentially just swaps out one screen for another, notably worse one.

Smart clothing is improving, but it could still use a decent tailor.

#4669. Do We Get More Generous as We Age?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Most of us are more willing to help people we feel close to. For example, we’ll give freely to a sibling, but think a little longer about a coworker, and hesitate more with someone we barely know. Psychologists call this social discounting — the value we place on another person’s welfare shrinks as social distance grows

A new study of adults in the United States and China suggests this economic phenomenon varies across age groups. For example, older adults are more generous to people with whom they have weaker social connections.

Yi Lu, an assistant professor of psychology at Western Kentucky University, set out to better understand if generosity varies across age. Lu earned her Ph.D. in developmental psychology at Cornell working with professor Corinna E. Löckenhoff, and collaborated on the study with colleagues at The Chinese University of Hong Kong and Peking University.

The research team asked nearly 1,000 adults of various ages from the U.S. and China to make a series of hypothetical decisions about how much money they would share with different people, from a close family member to a complete stranger. Participants also reported their charitable donations. The researchers then compared age groups while accounting for participants' cultural values and other background differences.

In both countries, older adults were the most generous. Compared with younger adults, they were less influenced by social distance (more willing to help acquaintances and strangers) and they gave more to charity.

Lu points out that many people assume older adults become more self-focused or simply have less to give as they age. But, she says, the data told a different story. Because the pattern appeared in two different cultural settings, it may reflect a broader pattern about how people change with age.

While both Chinese and American older adults were more likely to give than younger adults, there were some cultural differences. Regardless of age, people who placed greater value on equality and closeness with others tended to be more generous. Those who placed greater value on personal achievement and status tended to be less generous. Taken together, the findings suggest that generosity in adulthood reflects both how old we are and the values we hold.

Lu notes several limitations to this study. The questions were hypothetical, so they capture what people said they would do, not necessarily what they would do with real money in the moment; and the real charitable donations were self-reported. The study also compared people of different ages at one point in time. That shows older and younger adults differ in their generosity, but it doesn’t prove that people become more generous as they age, because generational differences may play a role.

The study also doesn’t explain why older adults give more, Lu notes. Researchers have some ideas, such as a shift toward emotionally meaningful goals later in life, but there isn’t concrete evidence that points to a reason.

“This is one of the few studies to look at how people of different ages share resources with others across social distances and across cultures,” Lu said. “In both the U.S. and China, older adults in our study were more willing to extend generosity beyond their close circle. That matters for how we think about aging. Older adults aren’t just recipients of support; they can be an important source of generosity in their communities.”

The take-home message: Older adults are more likely to give to people beyond their social circles than compared to younger adults. And no matter the age, people who value equality and closeness tend to be more generous overall.

#4668. Used EVs are suddenly hot sellers — Here are the top SUVs for under $25,000

Don’t want to pay full price? Used EVs with low miles, like the Hyundai IONIQ 5 and Ford Mustang Mach-E, are selling on the secondhand market for $25,000 or less.

With a flood of electric cars returning from lease this year and soaring gas prices, used EVs are suddenly flying off the lot.

Used EV sales rose to a record 3.3% of total used vehicle sales last month, up from 2.9% in August, according to Cox Automotive.

Used ICE vehicle sales, on the other hand, dropped 4.4% in September as buyers flocked to more efficient options.

As expected, Tesla remains the leading used EV brand, followed by Ford, Chevrolet, Hyundai, and BMW.

By model, the Nissan Ariya led growth, with sales up 42.5% in September, followed by the Chevy Equinox EV (+41.9%), Kia EV9 (+36.2%), and Chevy Blazer EV (+30.2%), while the Ford Mustang Mach-E (+14.7%) and Tesla Model Y (+13.8 %) also saw more demand.

With more options to choose from, which one is best for you? To help you decide, Edmunds, which has tested nearly all of them, put together a list of four top used electric SUVs available for under $25,000.

The first one on the list was the Chevy Equinox EV, or as GM used to call it, “America’s most affordable 315+ range” electric vehicle.

After it arrived in 2024, the Chevy Equinox EV quickly became one of the top-selling electric vehicles in the US outside Tesla, winning over buyers with enough space for a family and plenty of driving range at an affordable price.

The Chevy Equinox EV offers up to 319 miles of EPA-estimated driving range. It’s a great fit for those looking for a smaller, more efficient SUV that still offers plenty of interior space.

Edmunds says it’s worth upgrading to the 2LT trim, which adds heated front seats and a heated steering wheel, a wireless phone charger, adaptive cruise control, and a 360-degree HD Surround Vision camera system.

Next on the list was the Ford Mustang Mach-E, which has also remained a top seller since it went on sale in 2021.

Ford tapped into its iconic Mustang nameplate to help attract new buyers. The Mustang Mach-E came well equipped with a large 15.5″ infotainment screen with Wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto and Ford Co-Pilot360 Assist+.

While the GT is the most fun to drive, Edmunds said the Premium trim may be your best bet. It still offers plenty of performance while adding standard features like heated front seats and a heated steering wheel.

It’s also worth upgrading to the extended-range battery pack, which offers up to 320 miles of range on the Premium RWD model. You should be able to find used 2021 to 2023 Mach-E’s for under $25,000.

Another top-selling electric SUV, the Hyundai IONIQ 5 continues to win over buyers with its bold design, long-range capabilities, fast charging, and a surprisingly spacious interior.

Edmunds says plenty of used 2022 to 2024 IONIQ 5s with low mileage are available for under $25,000.

While the base SE Standard Range is the cheapest, it only offers an EPA range of 220 miles. Upgrading to the Extended Range battery, which is used on all other trims, provides up to 303 miles of range.

The Volkswagen ID.4 went on sale in the US in 2021 as one of the earlier mainstream electric SUVs.

It also just happens that many EVs are coming off lease so the inventory is plentiful combined with high gas price. Perfect storm.

It was updated in 2024, but up until the 2023 model year, the VW ID.4 offered an EPA range of up to 275 miles, depending on the configuration.

Finding a low-mileage used 2023 ID.4 shouldn’t be hard, but upgrading to the Pro S trim might be worth it.

Volkswagen updated the 2023 ID.4 with a new 12″ infotainment display and Park Assist Plus. The Pro S trim gained a fixed panoramic roof, V-Tex synthetic leather seating, and a heated steering wheel.

#4667. Spider named after Stephen Colbert has twice as many chromosomes as you

Published Oct 28, 2026 4:01 PM EDT

Stephen Colbert’s tenure as host of The Late Show sadly ended when CBS cancelled the historic series in May, but his 11-season run was only possible thanks to a prior gig. From 2005 to 2014, former The Daily Show alum played a larger-than-life, egotistical caricature of himself for Comedy Central’s The Colbert Report. In 2008, a team of entomologists even named newly discovered species of trapdoor spider after him: Aptostichus stephencolberti. And yes, the “t” in “stephencolberti” is silent.

It’s taken nearly 20 years, but researchers finally sequenced the arachnid’s entire genome. As they detailed in a study recently published in the Journal of Heredity, A. stephencolberti also boasts a biological detail that would make Colbert’s Comedy Central character proud. Even though it is only the size of a quarter, the northern Californian spider’s genetic sequence is about 50 percent larger than the genome of a human.

“At 4.6 gigabases, or 4.6 billion DNA base pairs, it’s not the largest genome among the spiders, but it’s significant,” said Jason Bond, a University of California Davis entomologist and study co-author.

Compared to the measly 23 in a human, A. stephencolberti features 53 chromosomes.. Over three-quarters of those are repetitive sequences instead of additional genes, but like all other spiders, it lacks telomere repeats. Telomere genes serve as the protective ends for chromosomes, and biologists theorize this may partially explain why spider chromosomes evolve so much faster than vertebrates.

“It lends itself to broadening our understanding of spider genome composition and consequently how genomes have evolved across the animal tree of life,” explained Bond.

A. stephencolberti lives along dunes that stretch from Monterey to the San Francisco Bay, with the females residing in silk-lined burrows. Vibrations alert them to nearby prey, which they ambush by springing from a hidden, hinged door. Although technically venomous, A. stephencolberti’s bite isn’t dangerous to humans. Like many animals, rising sea levels threaten to eradicate the spider’s current West Coast habitat, while invasive species pose additional dangers.

Bond and his colleagues weren’t aware of A. stephencolberti’s impressive genome when they first discovered and named it.. Instead, they were simply responding to Colbert’s self-parodying Comedy Central character. In 2008, the host specifically called out Bond on national television during his “Who’s Not Honoring Me Now?” segment after learning the researcher named a different trapdoor spider species after the rock musician Neil Young.

“And all I had to do was shamelessly beg on national television,” Colbert said at the time.

#4666. Sir Patrick Stewart Dies at 86 After Battle With Alzheimer's, Lewy Body Dementia

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Sir Patrick Stewart, best-known for portraying Captain Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek” and Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” film franchise, has died. He was 86.

The legendary actor and thespian passed away on October 28 after a “brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” according to his longtime spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter.

He died peacefully at his home in Los Angeles, where he was receiving care from his wife, Sunny Ozell.

“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” Bush Novak wrote in the statement. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”

Stewart’s acting career spanned more than six decades across theater, television, and film.

A longtime member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, he rose to international fame in 1987 with “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and later became known for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier in the 2000 film “X-Men” and its numerous sequels.

He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010 for his contributions to drama.

Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia are two progressive neurological conditions that can affect memory, thinking, behavior, and a person’s ability to perform everyday activities.

According to the National Institute on Aging (NIA), both conditions can cause dementia, a term used to describe a decline in cognitive abilities severe enough to interfere with daily life.

Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia. The condition is associated with abnormal buildups of proteins called amyloid and tau in the brain, which disrupt communication between nerve cells and contribute to their damage.

The NIA states that memory problems are often among the earliest symptoms of Alzheimer’s. As the disease progresses, people may experience increasing difficulty with language, reasoning, decision making, and recognizing familiar people.

Lewy body dementia, meanwhile, is associated with abnormal deposits of a protein called alpha-synuclein in the brain. These deposits, known as Lewy bodies, affect brain chemicals involved in thinking, movement, mood, and sleep, according to the NIA.

People with Lewy body dementia may experience changes in attention and alertness, visual hallucinations, muscle stiffness, difficulty walking, and sleep disturbances.

According to the Alzheimer’s Association, the two conditions may co-occur, and their overlapping symptoms may make diagnosis more challenging.

Currently, neither condition has a cure, but treatments are available to help manage symptoms. Certain medications can also slow cognitive decline in some people with early Alzheimer’s disease.

#4665. Dutch startup Elysian says electric flight may be closer than you think

They day you get to book an all-electric flight may be closer than you think if Dutch startup Elysian Aircraft gets its way. Their new E9X commercial airliner promises flights that are a whole lot quieter, and at prices that are whole lot less dependent on dumb oil wars.

Aircraft account for more than 2% of global heating when CO₂ and other emissions are taken into account, with the share considerably higher in wealthy countries, according to data cited by climate campaign group Stay Grounded. Elysian Aircraft is keenly aware of the industry’s climate impact, and they believe their planned full-size electric airliner will be perfectly positioned to make a dramatic difference.

“By being able to transport 90 passengers for initially 800 kilometers and eventually 1,000 kilometers you can reduce emissions to zero, from half the world’s flights,” Elysian co-founder Daniel Jacobson told EuroNews. “That is a very large amount of flight activity in the world. And you reduce total emissions from aerospace by 20%.”

At the core of those ambitious emission-reduction goals is the Elysian E9X aircraft. Designed in collaboration with aerospace researchers at Delft University of Technology (TU Delft), the E9X packs its oversized wings with modular battery packs, sending power to six propellers driven by electric motors.

Specs on those haven’t been revealed, but the E9X is designed to carry up to 100 passengers up to 1,000 km (~620 miles) from where they started. Elysian says that’s enough range to handle nearly 50% of scheduled commercial passenger flights worldwide and potentially eliminate 20% of total in-flight emissions when the plane enters service in 2034.

That said, the E9X is far more than “just a concept,” and Elysian has completed its second conceptual design review and flown a scaled demonstrator in concert with Germany’s DLR aerospace research center, demonstrating how its unique battery packaging solutions address the challenges of integrating heavy battery packs into an aircraft’s wings (where fuel is traditionally stored).

It’s interesting to see all the comments that point out the difficulties and problems associated with the introduction of battery powered aircraft into the mainstream industry. What none of them address is the industry’s obsession with cutting their operating costs no matter what pain passengers and flight crews must endure. My bet is if the airlines can save money by converting to battery powered aircraft—there are NO obstacles that will stop them from doing it. Battery electric aircraft may reduce operating costs by thousands of dollars per flight. That alone tells me that they will be flying passengers as soon as possible.

The company is also working with airline partners KLM and Transavia to explore the operational and commercial requirements for putting electric airliners into service, with aircraft lessor TrueNoord investigating how the E9X could be financed and supported commercially.

#4664. The Mental Edge: 6 Tools to Use to Perform Better at Anything

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Mental skills, also called psychological skills, are those mental abilities that allow us to do everything from getting up off the couch, getting through a rough day, managing a pressurized situation, and realizing our potential. These can be learned and honed to meet our individualized needs, and with practice, facilitate both small and large changes in our everyday and game time performance.

Want to be more motivated? Want to learn to handle stress better? Want to improve your run times? Want to start exercising? Want to do better on tests? Want more confidence? You get the idea. These skills can help.

Some foundational mental skills for performance optimization are deep breathing, relaxation skills, self-talk, a reset routine, cognitive reframing, and visualization/imagery.

Deep breathing is a foundational mental skill to incorporate into your mental skills playbook. Deep breathing is key to physical health, mental health, pain management, stress management, emotional control, and cognitive focus in high-stakes situations. Regularly practicing deep breathing is key to being able to use it during challenging moments to refocus and gain control of your physiological response.

There is a wide array of relaxation skills, but three effective ones are deep breathing, specifically diaphragmatic breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, and meditation. Relaxation techniques decrease stress and improve stress tolerance and improve health and cognitive performance.

For getting motivated, staying focused, and accomplishing goals, there is nothing quite like self-talk. That running dialogue in our heads is extremely powerful and feeds our self-confidence, attentional focus, problem solving abilities, and ability to stick with things even when they are hard. Instructional self-talk gives us the edge we need to remember how to execute complex problems or learn a new skill. If you have ever learned the breaststroke for example, you repeated the instructional mantra “pull, breathe, kick, glide” to yourself many times. Motivational self-talk, on the other, fuels our confidence, focus, and drive. “You got this!”

When we make a mistake or get thrown off our game by an external variable, sometimes we allow ourselves to be derailed. Performance suffers; we lose focus and become less effective. With a conscious reset routine at the ready to intervene, it is possible to rebound quickly and effectively. A good reset routine is short and incorporates an acknowledgment of the mistake or issue without judgment, a slow, deep breath, and a quick instructional self-talk cue to get back on track. For example, a flight student who has made a mistake during a training flight might 1) acknowledge the mistake without judgment, 2) take a deep 5-7 breath (inhale slowly for 5 counts, exhale slowly for 7 counts), and 3) refocus with the instructional self-talk cue, “Run the next checklist.” After a mistake on the field, an athlete might 1) acknowledge the mistake without judgement, 2) take a slow, deep breath, and 3) refocus with “Next play.”

Cognitive reframing involves recognizing maladaptive/self-defeating thoughts, examining them objectively, and reframing/replacing them with a realistic and practical thought. The goal here is not unrealistic positivity, but useful and task-focused language. For example, after a mistake during flight training, a student might think “I’m terrible, I’m going to fail out.” This thought is defeatist, absolute, and catastrophic. After examining the thoughts objectively, replacements might be: “I made a common mistake and need to refocus my study time on this area. I’ve worked hard to get here and otherwise I am doing well.” Cognitive reframing or restructuring has been shown to reduce self-critical rumination, increase positive affect, and decrease negative affect in athletes. Cognitive reframing can be used in the moment and is a valuable strategy to move forward after a setback.

Visualization and imagery are techniques in which we mentally simulate a task (e.g., emergency procedures or a golf swing) in order to better execute that task when needed. Mental rehearsal stimulates neurocognitive processes in much the same way as actually engaging in the activity. Visualization has been shown to enhance mental control, improve motor skills/technical skills and increase self-confidence, and can be used alone or in conjunction with other training strategies. Visualization, imagery, and mental rehearsal are key components of elite performers, including the Navy’s Blue Angels, who routinely engage in chair flying, in which maneuvers are mentally practiced in conjunction with motor movements (see The Blue Angels documentary, 2024, produced by Amazon MGM Studios).

Benefits of mental skills are that they are free, accessible to everyone, and have high levels of effectiveness, which can be applied to virtually any aspect of life. Whether your goal is to manage everyday stress, build confidence, bounce back from setbacks, earn your wings, win a championship, or perform at your best when it matters most, these skills can make a meaningful difference. Like physical skills, mental skills require practice to become effective and readily available when you need them. Start small, choose a skill or two that fits your needs, and practice consistently. Over time, you’ll build a mental skills playbook that you can make work for you.

#4663. The creepy science behind sleep paralysis ‘demons’

Published Oct 29, 2026 9:02 AM EDT

Have you ever woken up in the dead of night to find your limbs locked tight? Perhaps as you moved your eyes to the corner of your room, you spotted a demon lurking in the shadows, watching as you struggled against an invisible force. Sleep paralysis is creepy!

If you can take any comfort from your experience, it’s to know that sleep paralysis has a long and storied history of tormenting humanity. Why is sleep paralysis such a shared, spooky experience? And who exactly is that shadowy figure standing at the bottom of your bed?

Sleep paralysis affects slumberers around the world. Brian A. Sharpless, a clinical psychologist based in the Washington, D.C., area who has written multiple books on the phenomenon, says he has recorded more than 100 different terms for sleep paralysis across time, place, and culture.

While the fine details vary, the core experience is universal.  “Waking up, finding yourself unable to move, oftentimes a sense of pressure in the chest, a feeling of dread, fear, oppression. Those seem to be really consistent, but how you put a meaning on that is where it gets really interesting,” says Sharpless.

Historically, people often gave these experiences a supernatural origin. Sharpless says, in the West, sleep paralysis overlapped with stories about vampires, witches, and ghosts. In Germanic and Slavic folklore, a demon called a mare (which is the origin of our word “nightmare”) visited sleepers, sat on their chests, and paralyzed them.

As time passed, these associations changed to alien visitations or hazy “shadow people” lurking in the corners of their rooms. Since the 1960s, people in Tanzania have reported being attacked by a large winged creature called the Popobawa, which sexually assaults paralyzed victims.

But scientists also have explanations for sleep paralysis.

Sharpless says that a brain stuck between dreams and wakefulness produces this phenomenon. During REM sleep, one of the periods of rest when dreams are most likely, the brainstem paralyzes the body’s muscles, except, of course, those that move our eyes and keep us breathing. This is vital, as sleepers might otherwise act out their dreams and harm themselves or others.

But awakening while the body is still shut down is not pleasant. “It’s kind of an uncanny, strange experience not to have control over your body,” says Sharpless. As a result, surveys of people who have reckoned with sleep paralysis show it is almost always a fearful experience.

Another shared factor in sleep paralysis is feeling a presence in the room. These sleep paralysis demons, aliens, vampires, or Popobawas are generated by what researchers call the threat-activated vigilance system.

“What we think happens is that your brain is reading the sense that you’re prey, and it creates a predator,” says Sharpless.

Some people go through their whole lives without experiencing sleep paralysis, but some factors put you more at risk.

Sharpless says that people with a history of trauma or anxiety are more vulnerable. Sleep paralysis is also linked to being a student, consuming alcohol, or having narcolepsy. All of these factors are in turn linked to more disrupted sleep.

Sharpless says that, in general, poor sleep hygiene increases the risk of sleep paralysis. No randomized controlled trials, the gold standard for testing treatments, have been conducted for potential solutions to sleep paralysis, but Sharpless says interventions that improve sleep will likely also reduce the risk of sleep paralysis.

“One of the best, easiest things you can do is don’t drink before you go to bed and try to sleep on your side,” says Sharpless.

Sleeping on your back, he says, might make it slightly harder to breathe during sleep, especially in people who are overweight or obese. Sleep paralysis is less likely to happen to side sleepers, he adds. If a sleeper’s partner sees them sleeping on their back, gently moving them onto their side can reduce the chances of sleep paralysis.

Generally improving sleep hygiene, and getting treated for any anxiety, depression, or trauma, are also important steps, Sharpless says.

Sharpless has only experienced sleep paralysis once. In that episode, a terrifying face with sunken red eyes, balanced atop an improbably long neck, wound its way into his room. It was only when he remembered he had watched a documentary on sleep paralysis that very day that the fear, and then the face, dissipated.

He warns that there’s anecdotal evidence that sleep paralysis may be contagious. So, after reading this piece, sleep on your side, and if a demon appears in the corner of your room, remember it’s simply a figment of a tired, wired brain.

“Try to have a sense of humor about it,” advises Sharpless.

#4662. Obesity in Your 20s and 30s May Increase Cancer Risk Later in Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Younger adults with obesity may be more likely to develop cancer before midlife than those who maintain a moderate weight, according to a study published on October 26 in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

The risk for cancer became higher as weight increased. The highest rates were seen in those with severe obesity and abdominal obesity.

This highlights the potential importance of weight management in the prevention of early onset cancer.

Rates of both obesity and early onset cancer are rising among younger adults globally.

This study analyzed data from the Korean National Health Insurance Service database. The researchers identified 6,313,338 adults ages 20 to 39 who had no history of cancer and who underwent standardized national health screenings.

The researchers followed the participants for an average of 11 years.

Body mass index (BMI) was categorized into five groups ranging from underweight to class II obesity using the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria for Asian populations. Waist circumference was also measured as an indicator of abdominal adiposity.

During the analysis, the researchers adjusted for various factors such as:

Over the follow-up period, there were 151,893 cases of cancer among the participants. The incidence rate increased progressively based on obesity categories, from 1.84% in “normal-weight” individuals to 2.24% in class I obesity and 2.62% in class II obesity.

The strongest associations were seen in the following cancers:

Obesity was not associated with breast cancer diagnosed before the age of 50.

Ketan Thanki, MD, board certified colorectal surgeon with the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in Long Beach, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, explained to Healthline that obesity itself causes states that promote cancer formation.

This current study focused on the Korean population. However, the connection between obesity and cancer risk is a global issue.

Previous research has shown that around 10% of all new cancer diagnoses in the United States are associated with obesity. Obesity also accounts for up to 50% of certain cancers, including endometrial and liver cancer.

The study also showed that waist circumference, which indicates abdominal obesity, may be linked to cancer risk that is similar to that of individuals with overweight.

The study researchers used the thresholds set out by the Korean Society for the Study of Obesity. These thresholds put the waist circumference cutoff at over 90 cm (35.4 in) for males and over 85cm (33.46 in) for females.

These are not universal cutoffs. According to the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), waist circumference measurements that can increase your risk of negative health issues are 101.6 cm (40 in) for males and 88.9 cm (35 in) for females.

Previous research has also suggested an association between waist circumference and cancer risk, independent of BMI. One study showed a potential 11% increased risk of cancer in people with a waist circumference over the thresholds, even if they were physically active.

The current study found that males had a higher relative association between obesity and cancer, while females showed higher absolute risk.

The researchers also found that the absolute risk was higher in adults ages 30 to 39.

Those who currently smoke or who have ever smoked were also found to have a higher risk of developing cancer than those who have never smoked.

“Diet, exercise, and now medications can all be used very effectively to reduce one’s weight and, hopefully as a result, cancer risk,” Thanki said.

He also noted that, due to differences between South Korean populations and those in other countries such as the United States, further studies will be needed to determine how this translates across other populations.

“But I think this trend will likely extend across all cultures,” he said.
