#4619. Toyota Making the Land Cruiser's Cool Round Headlights Available After Purchase, But There's a Catch

J250 drivers can swap out their stock rectangular lights for the retro circular ones ... if they live in Japan.

The Toyota Land Cruiser has long been an enthusiast favorite, but the modern iteration arguably lacks some of its original charm—or at least, the amount it has might depend on what version you get and where you live. When the J250-generation Land Cruiser launched a few years back, Toyota linked its styling cues to trim level here in the United States Upscale trim Land Cruisers featured square headlights, while the base model Land Cruiser 1958 trim (as well as the First Edition) had rounded headlights. However, the 250 Series Land Cruiser only came with square headlights in many overseas markets.

Now, Toyota will offer a round headlight retrofit as an option on all 250-Series Land Cruisers. There is, however, a catch: at least for now, the add-on is only available in the Japanese market.

The replacement parts feature a taller lighting unit with circular LED daytime running lights with the Land Cruiser logo and larger amber indicators at the side. This helps fill front-end space, and aligns the light with the bottom edge of the grille. The new round headlight option will be available on Land Cruisers produced after April 2024 for ¥204,600, or $1296 at current exchange rates; his pricing includes installation.

And the round headlight design isn’t just cooler; it actually works better. Insurance Institute for Highway Safety testing revealed that the round design provides superior visibility compared to the squared-off design. Toyota Land Cruiser 1958 models earned a "good" rating with their round headlights, while Land Cruisers with square headlights only managed a “marginal" rating. Here’s hoping Toyota begins offering the after-market headlight upgrade here in the States, too.

#4618. GLP-1s May Help Lower Diabetes, Heart Risks Better Than Standard Prevention

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

GLP-1 drugs are more effective in helping prevent type 2 diabetes than the commonly prescribed medication metformin, according to a new study.

Researchers said GLP-1s such as Ozempic and Mounjaro were more likely to reduce blood sugar to healthy levels in people with prediabetes and obesity.

They added that people prescribed GLP-1 medications had a lower risk of progressing from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.

The researchers noted that GLP-1 users also had a lower risk of death from any cause as well as fewer heart attacks, strokes, and heart failure events compared with metformin users.

“The great news with prediabetes is that it’s still possible to reverse the progression of the disease,” said Vinicius de Sousa Barzon Serra, MD, a study author and research fellow in cardiovascular medicine at the Mayo Clinic in Scottsdale, Arizona, in a press release. “This research may add to the case for considering GLP-1 medications earlier for certain patients, rather than waiting until they develop type 2 diabetes.”

Serra noted that metformin still remains an effective treatment for people with prediabetes and type 2 diabetes.

“This is less about replacing one medication with another and more about discussing additional options with specific patients,” he said.

The researchers presented their findings at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago. The research has not been published yet in a peer-reviewed journal.

David Cutler, MD, a family medicine physician at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, wasn’t involved in the study, but said the findings were “quite impressive.”

“It elevates the comfort of prescribing GLP-1 drugs as a front-line treatment,” he told Healthline.

Robert Eckel, MD, a former president of the American Heart Association who was likewise not involved in the study, agrees the research provides more options for patients and prescribers.

“GLP-1s provide another option for prevention, perhaps as an add-on therapy. However, costs and access to these medications are important factors,” said Eckel, an endocrinologist at the University of Colorado School of Medicine, in the press release.

For their study, the researchers analyzed the medical records of 256,000 adults in the United States with prediabetes and obesity. About 76% of the subjects were women, and the average age of the participants was 52.

About half of those studied were taking GLP-1 drugs with the active ingredient semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide, or dulaglutide.

The other half had been prescribed metformin, a medication used to help manage blood sugar levels in adults and some children with type 2 diabetes by decreasing glucose production in the liver, reducing glucose absorption from food, and improving the body’s insulin sensitivity.

The researchers reported that the people in the study who were taking GLP-1 drugs had a 1.5 times higher chance of reversing high blood sugar to healthy levels compared to people who were using metformin.

The researchers also noted that GLP-1 medication users had a 31% lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes and a 41% lower risk of death from any cause.

They added that GLP-1 medications were associated with 15% fewer heart attacks, 20% fewer strokes, 25% fewer cases of heart failure, and 8% fewer cases of atrial fibrillation (AFib), a common type of irregular heartbeat.

The researchers cautioned that their study is observational and, therefore, cannot prove a cause-and-effect relationship. They also noted they relied on prescription records, so the frequency and dosage at which patients took their medication was not reflected.

In addition, the GLP-1 drugs were grouped together, so individual differences between medications were not considered.

Eckel said in the news release that the benefits for people taking GLP-1 drugs were probably mainly due to weight loss. Eckel noted that the research results open up a wide range of possibilities.

“This is an important finding because the GLP-1 receptor agonists are commonly used today and this is a population that in the transition from prediabetes to diabetes are at increasing risk for cardiovascular disease,” Eckel said in a taped interview alongside the study findings.

Cutler pointed out that several GLP-1 drugs also target blood sugar levels and insulin production. They could be effective in people with prediabetes who don’t have weight management issues.

Cutler noted that these people, however, might be reluctant to take GLP-1 drugs because they may not be experiencing symptoms of their prediabetes but could develop side effects with the medications.

“They would not be getting any immediate benefits,” Cutler said. He added that metformin, which was first used clinically in 1958, remains an effective alternative. “It’s been proven safe, effective, and it’s very cheap,” Cutler said.

It’s estimated that 40 million people in the United States have diabetes, with more than 90% of those cases being type 2 diabetes, a chronic condition characterized by high blood glucose levels that results from the body’s ineffective response to insulin or insufficient insulin production.

It’s also estimated that 115 million adults in the United States have prediabetes, a condition in which a person has higher-than-normal blood sugar levels but not high enough to be diagnosed as type 2 diabetes.

Around 5–10% of people with prediabetes develop diabetes every year. More broadly, up to 70% of people with prediabetes eventually develop diabetes.

Medication is sometimes prescribed for people with type 2 diabetes and prediabetes. Lifestyle changes can help reverse type 2 diabetes and prediabetes, as well as prevent the progression from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.

Cutler said the lifestyle changes needed to prevent type 2 diabetes are pretty clear.

“The most important thing for people with prediabetes to know is they should lose weight, reduce their carbs, exercise daily and, if that doesn’t work, then consider medication,” he said.

#4616. Mate Rimac’s Bugatti Chiron Was Stolen From the Factory After He Left the Keys Inside

The car was quickly tracked down, and the CEO now says he’ll stop leaving his keys inside his multi-million dollar hypercar.

Mate Rimac, by just about any definition, is a very smart man. After all, this is a man who arguably revolutionized the electric car as much as that fellow from South Africa who gets all the press; a man who created his own EV racer as a teenager, his own electric hypercar company before he was 22 years old, and explored the bleeding edge of high-end EVs so impressively that Porsche and the VW Group gave him the reins of Bugatti at the age of 33. (He is also a very polite, patient, and fun man, as I found while interviewing him at the Geneva Motor Show and he was game to do a Vanna White impression for camera to show off the Rimac Nevera.)

But we all have blind spots. One of his, apparently, involves occasionally leaving the keys to his own personal Bugatti Chiron in the car—and on Wednesday, that led to the in-hindsight-perhaps-obvious occurrence of someone stealing his multi-million dollar speed machine from the Rimac factory.

Rimac spilled the beans himself in a set of social media posts on Thursday, explaining exactly what happened. Croatia, he stresses, is a very safe place, so for years now, he’s been leaving his keys in his cars, be they his Nevera or his Chiron or whatever else. But while the buildings are secured, the compound is fairly open, which the CEO says enabled a stranger to wander in and take the car.

After some brief confusion as to whether someone authorized to take the car had borrowed it, Rimac says, he and his crew realized the Bugatti had been boosted, and called the police. As officers arrived, Rimac says he was tracking the Chiron from its on-board telemetry, and realized it was heading towards the Slovenian border. So, being awesome, the CEO gave chase in the Porsche 911 he happened to have on hand.

Rimac says the driver made it all the way to Austria before authorities there, aided by real-time updates from the factory, were able to stop the Bugatti. At the police station there, the CEO says the thief claimed he had actually come to the factory looking for a job, then saw the Chiron with the key inside— “Like it was my fault!”, Rimac says with astonishment—and then took off with the car. (Rimac says the man was planning to go to Germany “for whatever reason,” but I think we can all make a guess as to why.)

The second, perhaps even more dramatic post, showcased the security camera footage of the theft itself. In it, the apparently cigarette-smoking thief ever-so-slowly sidles up to the blue Bugatti, glancing around before eventually taking one final drag and clambering into the car. The CEO wisely went for “The Pink Panther Theme” as a soundtrack here, but the Parks & Recreation “Don’t Be Suspicious” song would work just as well.

Suffice it to say, Rimac says he will not be keeping the keys in the cars from now on. “Don’t try your luck—it will not happen again,” he says.

#4614. Low-Calorie Diet and Supervised Exercise May Reverse Early Onset Type 2 Diabetes

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

The RESET for Remission trial, presented at the 2026 European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) Annual Meeting and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas on October 1, found that more than half of adults with early onset type 2 diabetes entered remission after six months on a low calorie diet and supervised exercise program.

Early onset type 2 diabetes is when the condition is diagnosed before age 45.

Those with early onset type 2 diabetes may be at a higher risk of complications like long-term damage to the capillaries (microvascular complications), adverse cardiovascular outcomes, and earlier death.

Typical treatment for early onset type 2 diabetes is often a combination of lifestyle changes, like diet and exercise, and medications.

However, this new study suggests that a supervised low calorie diet and exercise program may help some people with early onset type 2 diabetes enter remission.

The RESET for Remission trial included 96 adults from England and Canada who were between the ages of 18 and 45, had early onset type 2 diabetes, obesity, and were not on insulin treatment.

The participants had an average age of 38 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 35.2 kg/m2. They were randomized into a control group that received usual care alone and the intervention group, which ate a low calorie diet and participated in supervised exercise programs.

During the first 12 weeks, participants in the intervention group followed an 800–900-calorie-per-day diet and completed twice-weekly supervised aerobic and resistance exercise sessions, along with one independent exercise session per week.

For weeks 13–24, they transitioned to a weight-maintenance diet and independent exercise.

Both groups were supervised by physicians, and the intervention group was also closely supervised by licensed dietitians.

The low calorie diet consisted of 30% protein, 50% carbohydrate, and 20% fat. Participants were also encouraged to drink at least 2 liters of calorie-free fluids per day and given access to a fiber-based laxative as needed.

In the first two weeks, all meals were replaced with specially formulated nutritional products (Optifast). Then, in weeks 3–12, the participants maintained the same calorie intake but had more flexibility in their food choices.

This second phase of the diet included one conventional meal per day, with daily intake targets that included protein, fruit, and vegetables. Typically, this meant 60 to 90 grams of protein from all sources combined, one portion of fruit, and two portions of non-starchy vegetables.

At the end of 24 weeks, 54% of the intervention group entered remission of type 2 diabetes, compared with only 4% in the control group. Researchers defined remission as an HbA1c level below 6.5% without glucose-lowering medication for at least 12 weeks.

“This study proves what most physicians have advocated for quite some time. Clearly, diet and exercise can work to improve or even resolve diabetes,” David Cutler, MD, board certified family medicine physician at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline.

Cutler also added that this study provides a clear example of how difficult it can be to enter diabetes remission with diet and exercise alone. He stated that the small number of participants in the study also makes him wonder if these findings can be applied to all populations.

Another limitation of this study, as Cutler pointed out, was that the strict dietary limits imposed on study participants would be very difficult for the average adult to adhere to.

The study also followed participants for only six months, so it’s unclear how many would remain in remission over the longer term.

“It is worth trying diet and exercise first because they can work to achieve meaningful weight loss and remission of diabetes,” he said.

It may be possible to prevent or delay the onset of type 2 diabetes by:

The National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK) notes that losing 5%–7% of your body weight can help reduce your risk of type 2 diabetes.

Early onset type 2 diabetes is a growing issue worldwide, coinciding with the rise of obesity.

Research from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) projects that the number of people in the United States under age 20 with type 2 diabetes could reach 220,000 by 2060. This is an increase of 700%.

People diagnosed with type 2 diabetes at a younger age face more decades of living with the condition, along with a higher risk of developing complications earlier in life and reduced life expectancy. These complications can develop as early as midlife and include:

Speak with a healthcare professional about your risk of type 2 diabetes and changes you might be able to make in order to prevent or delay diagnosis.

A later diagnosis can help reduce the risk of some complications of the condition.

#4612. November skygazing: Planetary alignments, a supermoon, comet, and more

Published Oct 31, 2026 9:00 AM EDT

Autumn is here! The air is crisp, the leaves are falling, and the sky is alive. November brings a whole gamut of celestial phenomena for stargazing enthusiasts from a  planetary prom to a meteor shower that can explode occasionally into the most spectacular of sky shows, and  a comet that won’t return for 21 years Let’s get to it!

Mercury is generally difficult to spot. It’s our solar system’s smallest planet and is often lost in the sun’s haze. But in the middle of this month, this speedy boy is flitting in to join the party that Venus, Mars, and Jupiter are throwing all month. The three larger planets will be in alignment for all of November, festooning the morning sky just before  dawn. Venus will be in the southeastern sky, with Mars high in the eastern sky and Jupiter a bit lower, but also towards the east. And Mercury? Look low in the southeast, and it should be visible just before the sun emerges over the horizon.

As the month continues, Mars and Jupiter will edge closer and closer to one another, casting shy glances at one another across the sky like teenagers at a school dance. They’ll finally slide in for a waltz just before sunrise on November 16, where their conjunction in the eastern sky will be chaperoned by the bright star Regulus. Look to the east, but make sure you stop looking once the sun begins to peek its way into the firmament. No planetary conjunction is worth cooking your eyes.

And once the music stops and Mars and Jupiter will slip gracefully away, the fireworks will begin. The Leonids will be visible all month, but their peak is predicted for November 18. At that time, their radiant point—the point from which the meteors appear to emerge—will be right next to the two disengaging dancers in the constellation Leo. This shower usually produces 10 to 15 meteors per hour. However, in 1966 it exploded into one of the most spectacular displays of celestial pyrotechnics ever seen, with thousands of meteors visible every minute. So you never know what you might see!

This month’s full moon is the first of three consecutive supermoons. As per the ever-indispensable Farmer’s Almanac, it will reach peak illumination while below the horizon at 9:50 a.m. EST on November 24. When  actually visible, it’ll appear brightest on the evenings of November 23 and 24. This month’s moon takes its name from the industrious, dam-building rodents of North America, whose long summers of hard work start to pay off in November, when they retreat to their lodges to wait out the winter. Several other Indigenous nations have names that also refer to what animals get up to during the fall: the Tlingit call it the Digging Moon, to the Algonquin it’s the Whitefish Moon, while the Dakota and Lakota call it the Deer Rutting Moon.

The final event of November: a visit from Comet 161P/Hartley–IRAS. The space rock  will reach perihelion—the point at which it’s closest to the sun—on November 27. At that point, its magnitude will be about 12, which means you’ll want a decent telescope to spot it. The International Comet Quarterly suggests at least using a telescope with at least a 7.8 inch (20 centimeter) aperture. If you’ve got such an apparatus, look to the east-northeast, just above the horizon.

Remember that you’ll get the best experience gazing up at the stars if you get away from any sources of light pollution. You should also give your eyes plenty of time adjust to the darkness, and review our stargazing tips before heading out into the night.

#4611. Tested: 2027 BMW M350 xDrive Is Fast But Not Furious

Behind the Neue Klasse design, the eighth-generation 3-series gets the basics right.

The BMW 3-series is no longer the company’s best-selling car in the United States, but it is still the model closest to the formula that earned the brand its success and status with American enthusiasts. The all-new G50 is the eighth generation of 3-series and will be reaching the U.S. next year, with buyers initially able to choose between a four-cylinder 330 and an inline-six-powered M350 xDrive. It’s the latter, in European specification, that’s being tested here. Is this still the heart of the BMW brand?

Another product of BMW’s Neue Klasse era, the new 3-series gets radical new styling that closely aligns it with the fully electric i3 that will be sold alongside it (which we test separately here). But don’t let the looks fool you—beneath the surface, the two cars sit on different architectures and have subtly different dimensions. The gasoline-powered version is fractionally shorter and sits on a 112.6-inch wheelbase, 1.5 inches less than the EV’s.

The new M350 effectively replaces the previous G20-generation M340i, using a version of BMW’s long-serving B58 turbocharged inline-six that works in conjunction with a 48-volt mild hybrid system. This makes 437 horsepower and 428 lb-ft of torque, increases of 55 hp and 59 lb-ft over the outgoing car.

Drive is delivered through an eight-speed automatic transmission and an xDrive-branded all-wheel system as standard. The option of rear-wheel drive is no longer available. BMW plans to offer a switchable rear-wheel drive mode, but this wasn’t on the car R&T tested in France, as the company plans to introduce it later though a software update.

Our expert editors test every vehicle we review. Read more about how we test and review cars here.

Transmission: eight-speed automatic, all-wheel drive

The presence of BMW’s famous M badge on any model still raises expectations, even knowing that the M350 xDrive is a member of the M Performance range, essentially a diffusion line that sits beneath the fully-fledged M cars that keep single digits. The fact it has more power and torque than the F80-generation M3, which was on sale as recently as 2018, increases anticipation further.

The good news is the new car absolutely delivers on raw performance. BMW claims a 3.9-second 0–60-mph time, one that is almost certain to be substantially bettered with the scientifically applied brutality of instrumented testing. And the car feels every bit as quick as that number suggests, launching with M-appropriate seriousness and with huge, linear urge that barely diminishes as speeds turn extra-legal. It sounds good too, with a snarling exhaust note that proved to be mostly organic even when I deactivated the switchable active noise enhancement, but which wasn’t intrusive or droning at cruising speeds.

At lower revs there is a hint of turbo lag, the hybrid system not bringing enough punch to cancel this out, but the quick-shifting gearbox means I had to hunt this down by using the transmission’s manual mode to keep revs low. But out of the box, it feels like a substantial performance upgrade over the outgoing G20-generation M340i.

All the horses and pounds of twist are delivered to the road with a minimum of drama. On my test route in the south of France, the M350 punched out of tight corners without a hint of slip, only the combination of big throttle openings with high cornering loads creating any sense that the majority of power was traveling to the rear wheels. The M350’s dynamic brain kept everything under tight control, and while the forthcoming Drift Moment mode will doubtless unlock a wilder side to the car’s character, but on dry, smooth asphalt the lateral-g loadings generated by the Bridgestone Potenza tires were high enough that I didn’t feel any urge to go and explore the limits of grip on a tight mountain road.

Of course, the presence of occasional, accessible drama has long been a core part of the appeal of punchier M-branded BMWs, and on first impressions, this definitely felt to be lacking. The different dynamic modes did change the M350’s demeanor, with Sport and Sport Plus adjusting throttle mapping and steering weight. But none turned it into a party animal. This is one of those cars that is all business. The combination of true excitement and a gasoline engine will likely require waiting for the forthcoming combustion G84 M3, which will ultimately sit alongside the EV version.

It’s been a long while since steering excellence came as standard on most BMW models. Although the M350’s slightly ovoid steering wheel delivered crisp, linear front-end responses, actual feedback was muted and only present at all once the firm hand of the active lane-keeping system was turned off. The car felt stable and impressively precise in faster corners, but at lower speeds, the assistance weighting was too soft for my tastes in all its switchable modes.

The gentler side of the M350’s personality earns unstinted praise. Ride quality has improved markedly over the M340i, with the new car’s adaptive dampers dealing with every road surface I could find to throw at them. Beyond the engine noise—which is definitely a plus—the cabin stayed impressively quiet for a sports sedan, one area where BMW had clearly transferred learning from its well-insulated EVs. And the Highway Assistant system, a hands-off Super Cruise–style enhanced cruise control, kept the car centered in its lane, reacted to other vehicles intelligently, and even executed lane changes in response to a turn signal input. I did only a few kilometers of high-speed French Autoroute, but it was enough to show the M350 will be a relaxed, high-speed cruiser.

While the combustion 3-series isn’t an EV, it has an EV’s interior. Barring minor details the cabin architecture is identical to that of the i3, and while that means an abundance of technology it has also brought compromises.

BMW’s new “Panoramic Vision” is front and center. Literally, the narrow projection band that sits between dashboard and windshield goes the whole width of the cabin, serving as an elongated gauge cluster. The shape of this showstopping display is not naturally suited to the needs of a combustion car, with a tiny fuel gauge all the way to one side and the M350’s rev counter being a narrow strip in front of the driver where two graphic bars move away from each other as the engine spins faster. This lacked the simple clarity of a conventional rev counter, and while it is possible to place a rendered tacho into one of the panoramic screen’s reconfigurable slots, the display’s lack of height means this was small and hard to see.

Other elements that can be added include images of some of BMW’s classic Art Cars and a rendered M badge. Which is cool but emphasizes how much more room is on the display than there strictly needs to be. Making full use of the commendable lowness of the new car’s seating position also meant the top of the rim obstructed the part of the Panoramic Vision display unless the wheel was adjust to be a little low.

The primary touchscreen is the same diagonal-edged 17.9-inch one that we’ve already seen in the iX3 and the new X5, this running the latest BMW X operating system. This generally worked well, making it pretty easy to find more commonly used functions, although with the need to go mining through submenus and scrollable pages to reach minor ones. There is a permanently rendered line of heating and ventilation controls at the base of this display, but the temperature controls are small and fiddly to operate. And, like the iX3, the angle of the new 3’s air vents need to be adjusted using the touchscreen, making something that should be simple needlessly complex.

Interior space has been improved compared with the previous generation, with ample head and shoulder room up front and plentiful seat adjustment, along with a more obvious upgrade in the back, where occupants enjoy more legroom. This isn’t a car many would choose for regularly transporting full-size adults over long distances, but a six-footer could sit behind another six-footer, with both in reasonable comfort. Trunk space is 11.3 cubic feet, only fractionally less than the Mercedes C-class.

The M350’s M badge also earns it the M Sport steering wheel rather than the strangely styled four-spoke wheel that will go into the regular car. This looks better but still has a heavily thickened rim on each side, which makes it look like a halfway-evolved yoke. It was a little unwieldy when making inputs requiring more than a turn of lock. Some hidebound traditionalists might prefer their steering wheels to be, you know, round.

The existence of a nearly visually identical BMW i3 asks the most obvious question for those considering the gasoline-powered version. In its basic 50 form, the EV is slightly less expensive—$62,850 to the M350 xDrive’s $67,250, both of those including destination. Admittedly, the forthcoming i3 M60 is probably the closer comparison, but BMW hasn’t released pricing for that one yet.

Direct combustion rivals are thin on the ground at the moment. The Audi S5 is no longer, technically, a sedan, and is down on power compared with the BMW. And we’re still waiting for details on how AMG is planning to replace the C43 in the freshly revised lineup.

But anybody arriving at M350 ownership directly from an M340i is going to feel like they have received a substantial upgrade, that delivered in terms of performance, technology and practicality. We will get used to BMW's radical new direction in time, and the basics are all solid.

A welcome return to the quad exhaust tailpipes that BMW lost by hiding the M340i’s exhaust within shaped finishers integrated into the bumper. Even a junior M car deserves to have its pipes standing loud and proud.

#4610. Rivian (RIVN) Q3 2026 earnings: revenue up 38%, R2 now its best-seller

Rivian (RIVN) just released its Q3 2026 earnings, with revenue up 38% year-over-year to $2.155 billion. The R2, in its first full quarter of deliveries, is already the company’s best-selling vehicle, ahead of both the R1 and the Amazon van.

The results beat Wall Street’s expectations, and Rivian is raising its 2026 guidance on every metric. But the car business is still losing money, and the R2 ramp made the automotive margin worse this quarter.

We already had the volume side. Rivian reported earlier this month that it built 19,751 vehicles and delivered 19,248 in the quarter, both records. Deliveries were up 46% from a year ago and 58% from Q2.

Analysts were looking for about $2.02 billion in revenue, an adjusted loss of $0.61 per share, and an adjusted EBITDA loss of roughly $576 million, according to Bloomberg consensus. Rivian beat all three.

The demand signals for the R2 are good. Rivian says reservation conversion for the launch edition trim stayed above its expectations, it added a second R2 production shift in Normal, Illinois, and demo drives jumped to over 103,000 in the quarter, up from 57,000 in Q2.

The problem is the automotive gross margin. Rivian’s automotive segment posted an $80 million gross loss in Q3, a -5% margin. That’s better than the $130 million loss a year ago, but worse than the $36 million loss (-3%) we saw in Q2.

Rivian blames about $120 million of extra cost of revenue on the R2 ramp, compared to production at “more normalized levels.” And the quarter got help that won’t repeat on demand: $81 million in regulatory credit revenue and an IEEPA tariff refund receivable.

Strip out the credits and the automotive segment lost about $161 million at the gross level, or roughly $8,400 per vehicle delivered. Not great.

But there’s real progress under that. Rivian says automotive cost of goods sold per unit fell by more than $12,000 quarter-over-quarter thanks to the higher R2 mix and better fixed-cost leverage. Our own math from the filing puts it at about $84,700 per vehicle in Q3, down from $96,700 in Q2. Revenue per vehicle is coming down too, which is the point of a cheaper car: about $76,300 excluding credits, versus $85,000 in Q2.

The only reason Rivian posted a consolidated gross profit is its software and services segment, which brought in $605 million in revenue and $256 million in gross profit, a 42% margin.

Of that segment revenue, $354 million (59%) came from the joint venture with Volkswagen Group, which pays Rivian for electrical architecture and software development work. Rivian says it expects to recognize that revenue through about mid-2028. Autonomy+, the paid driver-assist package launched in April, is also in there, and Rivian says take rates are “trending ahead of our expectations.”

With 41,807 deliveries through September, Rivian needs between 25,193 and 28,193 in Q4 to land in the new range. That would be another record by a wide margin. Rivian is providing this guidance a month into the quarter, which gives strong confidence it will hit at leat the lower end of that target.

The capex cut is about “timing of spend,” not savings. Phase 1 of the Georgia plant, which is supposed to add 300,000 units of annual capacity for R2 and R3, is still under construction.

On cash, Rivian ended the quarter with $5.502 billion, or $7.095 billion in total liquidity once you add its credit facility and the $1 billion term loan Volkswagen funded in October. That’s after the $1.5 billion share sale in July. Free cash flow was -$1.124 billion in Q3 alone.

This is a good quarter for Rivian, and the R2 is clearly working. Becoming the best-selling Rivian within one full quarter, while the ramp is still early, is about as good a start as you could ask for. We saw the R2 roll off the line in April, and the demand side has held up since.

But be careful with the headline beat. A lot of it came from outside the car business: Volkswagen’s checks, regulatory credits, and a one-time tariff refund. The thing Rivian actually builds and sells lost more money at the gross level than it did last quarter.

Picked my R2 up a week ago and I’m already in love. It was worth the two year wait! I find myself looking for excuses to jump in and go for a joy ride.

Rivian is going to sell a metric ton of the lower cost versions.

The number we care about most is the $12,000 drop in cost per vehicle. If that keeps going as the second shift fills and the $120 million in ramp costs fade, the automotive segment can get to breakeven on its own. If it stalls, Rivian is a software contractor for VW with a money-losing car company attached.

I am betting on the former. With a shift added right before the quarter started, production will likely increase significantly in Q4, and Rivian already has strong visibility into demand a month into the quarter.

If anything, I’m impressed by the demand Rivian is seeing for the more expensive launch edition of the R2. It bodes well for the cheaper version, as long as it manages to get its cost down over the coming months.

#4609. 3 things you might not know about daylight saving time

Published Oct 31, 2026 1:39 PM EDT

Heads up: The clocks are about to change. The evening of Halloween gets an extra hour as the clocks fall back an hour, meaning you can sleep in on Sunday, November 1.

Complaints about daylight savings are as old as daylight savings itself, and pretty much everyone has an opinion about the practice. As with any such topic, there are all kinds of myths and misunderstandings out there.

This one comes up a lot: the idea that farmers are the reason we have daylight savings. In this version of the story, farmers, who work outside and need to align their workdays with the daylight, were the ones who made the argument for the practice.

In truth, farmers were the main group opposed to daylight savings during World War I. According to the Library of Congress: “The agriculture industry fervently opposed the measure because farming schedules are based on sunrise and sunset not the clock.”

After the war there was a bill to repeal daylight savings, which passed through both houses of Congress. President Woodrow Wilson vetoed that bill, and his statement about the veto acknowledged this wouldn’t make farmers happy.

“I realize the very considerable and in some respects very serious inconveniences to which the daylight-saving law subjects the farmers of the country,” he wrote. Wilson sided with the industrial sector. The veto was overridden, leading to a long period where daylight savings was practiced only in certain areas. For example: New York City observed daylight savings, but rural areas in New York State did not (not what you’d expect if farmers broadly supported daylight savings).

None of this is to say that some farmers don’t support daylight savings time today—it’s just that farmers aren’t the reason the practice exists in America. If anything, they tried to stop it.

There are some “facts” repeated so often that hardly anyone questions them, and “Ben Franklin invented daylight savings time” remains one of them. The problem is that it’s not true.

I’d understand if you’re skeptical—I’m a Canadian journalist trying to steal an achievement from one of America’s founding fathers. But you don’t have to take my word on this one—The Franklin Institute, a museum dedicated to Franklin’s legacy, states that “Daylight saving time is one thing that Franklin did not invent.” The United States didn’t even implement daylight savings until 1918, well over a century after Franklin passed away.

So where did the idea that he invented it come from? Probably from a satirical Journal de Paris article Franklin penned back in 1784.

In that piece he jokingly encouraged the residents of Paris to wake up earlier in the morning, in order to spend less money on candles. He also proposed a tax on shutters, rationing of candles, a prohibition of carriages on the streets after sunset, and church bells ringing at the crack of dawn every day. He, it goes without saying, wasn’t being entirely serious.

So where did the idea for daylight savings come from? New Zealand entomologist George Hudson first proposed intentionally shifting the clock in an 1895 talk to the Wellington Philosophical Society, then followed up with a paper in 1898.

This isn’t a myth, exactly, but it is something that rarely comes up in contemporary discussions about daylight savings. Multiple US states have proposed doing away with standard time entirely. Nationally, the Sunshine Protection Act, which passed the House over the summer, would institute the change from sea to shining sea.

Here’s the thing, though: this isn’t the first time. The US tried making daylight savings permanent during the height of the 1970s energy crisis. The problem was that people hated it. What was supposed to be a two-year experiment lasted less than a year because of a massive change in public opinion.

Support for the change started high, as an October 1974 New York Times article lays out: 79 percent of the public favored the idea in December of 1973, but by February of 1974, that dropped to 42 percent—a 37-point swing. A bill to restore standard time in winter passed the House by a 362 to 16 vote.

What caused the backlash? Dark winter mornings. Particularly prominent were complaints from parents, who didn’t like their children walking to school in the dark.

A 1975 study by the US Department of Transportation concluded that a year-round switch possibly isn’t a great idea, proposing instead a schedule change. “We conclude that modest overall benefits might be realized by a shift from the historic 6-month DST system (May through October) to an 8-month DST system (March through October),” the paper concludes. This, notably, is pretty much what the US has been doing since 2007.

The past isn’t a prediction of the future—it’s possible switching to year-round daylight savings would go differently today. Walking to school is less common, for one thing, and streets are better lit. All the same, it’s worth realizing this has been tried before.

#4607. Toyota’s EV sales more than doubled in a year, but gas cars are getting crushed in China

Toyota’s EV sales have jumped 127% through September, but that isn’t telling the whole story. Slumping demand for gas and hybrid cars in China has pushed global sales lower for three months in a row.

Including Lexus, Toyota sold 309,766 battery electric vehicles (BEVs) globally through the first nine months of 2026, up 127.4% from the same period last year.

Except for January (+87.5%), Toyota’s EV sales have more than doubled every month this year compared with 2025.

The higher demand comes after Toyota and Lexus launched updated versions of their first-gen electric SUVs, the bZ4X (now the bZ in the US) and the RZ.

Toyota has added several new electric models, including the C-HR+ (C-HR in the US), bZ4X Touring (bZ Woodland in the US), and Urban Cruiser, while Lexus now offers the ES EV. Both brands will introduce a three-row electric SUV, which is expected to go on sale over the next few months.

According to data from Cleantechnica, the Toyota bZ4X became the 20th best-selling EV worldwide through August, with nearly 100,000 units sold.

While its EVs are catching on, Toyota Motor’s global sales fell for the third straight month in September.

Toyota sold 860,107 vehicles in September, down 2.2% from the previous year. The company said that although overall demand remained steady, sales in China fell, leading to lower overall sales than last year.

Through September, Toyota sold 7.51 million vehicles globally, down 3.4%. In China, Toyota’s sales plunged nearly 20%, marking its eighth consecutive month with lower sales.

Toyota said the overall market in China “remained weak due in part to rising gasoline prices, while the market for gasoline vehicles and hybrid vehicles was particularly affected,” resulting in lower sales.

In the first nine months of 2026, Toyota sold just over 1.05 million vehicles in China, 18.9% fewer than in the same period last year.

Toyota sells several electric vehicles through its two joint ventures (GAC Toyota and FAW Toyota) in China, including the bZ3, bZ3X, bZ5, and bZ7.

After the US, China is Toyota’s second-largest market. Through September, Toyota has now sold more vehicles in its home market of Japan (1.19 million) than in China.

To turn things around and compete with companies like BYD, Toyota, like many major OEMs nowadays, is increasingly adopting more Chinese EV tech and manufacturing practices.

Nikkei reported in August that Toyota plans to build a new Lexus electric SUV in China, rather than in Japan as it has traditionally. Production is expected to begin at Lexus’ new manufacturing plant in Shanghai next fall.

Toyota's EV sales still represent less than 3% of its overall sales. This is the real news.

BTW, Toyota's European sales got hit in a similar way. They are up 0,7% YoY but that's compared to a rising overall market of 5,7%. This lead to it's market share shrinking.

The new Lexus EV will use advanced manufacturing methods, including gigacasting, to cut costs and speed up production.

Toyota isn’t the only legacy automaker struggling to keep pace in China’s fast-moving automotive market.

Volkswagen Group CFO and COO, Arno Antilitz, admitted the company “must act quickly and decisively” after reporting third-quarter sales in China dropped 38% to 405,800 units on Thursday. The company also plans to use technology developed in China for its next-gen EVs, which it will sell overseas.

#4606. What to do if you hit a deer

Published Oct 31, 2026 2:07 PM EDT

When you think of the fall season, chances are that gorgeous foliage, brisk sweater weather, and Halloween decorations come to mind. Deer, on the other hand, think of sex.

Deer breeding behavior, known as the rut, aligns with the changing length of daylight. As daylight decreases, buck (male deer) and doe (female deer) hormones increase. While in southern states the rut can last several months, it only runs for a short period of time during the fall in the Northeast.

During the rut, bucks seek out does that are ready to breed, and the amorous pursuit can be intense. Because some bucks are so obsessed with breeding, they can eat little and burn through up to 20 percent of their body weight during the season. And just like love-crazed high schoolers, deer during the rut are more distracted and less cautious, as well as more active during the day than they usually are.

“During this period, many yearling bucks leave their birth areas in search of new territory, sometimes dozens of miles away. At the same time, adult bucks are actively roaming their home ranges in pursuit of doe, often chasing those they encounter,” according to Raven Ridge Wildlife Center in Pennsylvania.

What’s more, “The end of daylight-saving time means more vehicles will be on the road during dusk and dawn, which are the peak hours for deer movement.”

In fact, most deer-vehicle accidents take place in October through December. While there are things you can do to lessen your chances of hitting one—such as staying alert and paying close attention when you see deer crossing signs—sometimes accidents are unavoidable. So what should you do if you hit a deer?

Safely pull over and turn your emergency flashers on. While your instinct might be to go see the deer or move the body off of the road, resist the temptation. Care for any injured passengers, and call 911. The dispatchers will send the appropriate authorities to help.

And if you narrowly avoided one deer, remember that, “deer often travel in groups and walk single file,” per the Raven Ridge Wildlife Center. “So even if one deer successfully crosses the road in front of a driver, it doesn’t mean the threat is over. Another could be right behind it.”

#4605. Putrid blood shoots from these lizards’ eyes

Published Nov 1, 2026 8:03 AM EST

Horned lizards are spiky cuties. Three to six inches long, these lizards are coated with sharp spines all across their hard, sand-colored backs. But in the dry deserts and prairies they call home, they are still vulnerable. As they scuttle through the protective brush in arid landscapes from Mexico to southern Canada, they have to reckon with hungry coyotes, snakes that will gobble them whole, and even peckish roadrunners. That’s why multiple species of horned lizards have developed a weird but effective deterrent: blood.

And not just any blood: These lizards shoot foul-smelling blood out of their eyes, sending many would-be predators scattering. But experts say the lizards are now facing other threats to their survival that even a fountain of eye blood can’t deter.

Dean Williams, a professor of biology at Texas Christian University, studies horned lizard populations in central Texas. He says that blood squirting is really a backup defense for the lizards. “Their first line of defense is going to be crypsis,” aka blending in with their background, says Williams.

Williams and his colleagues tag the lizards they study with radio trackers that pinpoint their location to an area roughly the size of an office desk. Even then, he says, it can take “15 minutes of rummaging” to find the lizard in their scrubland habitat. The lizards don’t move much, he added, blending in with nearby rocks.

But when hiding doesn’t work, the lizards deploy their unusual, foul-smelling blood, which Williams says is a product of an equally foul delicacy. “Their diet consists mainly of these large Pogonomyrmex or harvester ants,” says Williams. Harvester ants defend themselves using neurotoxic venom that causes intense, long-lasting, stinging pain in mammals.

Unfortunately for the harvester ants, this toxin doesn’t even slightly deter horned lizards, who eat the ants in large numbers. A 2024 study identified that a compound in the lizards’ blood spiked after scientists fed them harvester ants. The researchers think this compound, possibly adapted from ant venom, makes the lizards’ blood taste foul.

However, that gross metabolized ant blood coursing through the lizards’ veins wouldn’t be much help if it only annoyed a predator after it had already bitten off the lizard’s head. That’s where the lizards’ unusual squirting mechanism comes in handy.

Williams explains that the lizards can build up pressure in blood vessels around their sinuses. Eventually, the vessels burst, shooting the toxic blood out in jets. Mammals exposed to the stream of blood react with notable disgust. There seems to be little consequence for the lizards, even though in one experiment, a lizard lost 6.8 percent of its body mass after squirting blood when exposed to a dog.

The foul-smelling blood doesn’t protect the lizards from every predator, though. Roadrunners and other birds of prey still chow down on them, says Williams. To guard against birds, the lizards use the sharp horns on the back of their heads to stab at predators that try to seize them in their beaks.

The lizards’ foul blood also does little to deter snakes. Instead, the lizards have evolved specialized strategies to evade these predators. Rattlesnakes are lazy hunters that wait in the shadows for prey to approach. Horned lizards have learned to run away from these snakes.

But Williams says they use a different strategy if hunted by a coachwhip or racer snake. These fearsome snakes can easily chase down the lizards, who instead quickly flatten their bodies against the dirt, showing the snake their spiked backs, which makes them harder to swallow.

But despite these bespoke, often ingenious defense mechanisms, horned lizards in the Lone Star State are under serious threat. They’ve disappeared from their habitat across eastern Texas. Williams says that industrialization is devastating lizard populations. “They seem to be very sensitive to those habitat changes,” he says.

In small towns, the lizards can live alongside humans when their natural brush habitat is preserved. But in towns where humans cleared the brush, “the lizards just disappeared,” Williams says.

Horned lizards are ectotherms, meaning they must change their behavior to keep their body temperature under control. In the blistering heat of a Texas summer, the lizards simply can’t keep their bodies within safe limits once the cool shade of vegetation has disappeared.

Harvester ants provide horned lizards with one of their strongest defenses. But another ant species has become the second major challenge to the lizards’ survival. Fire ants are an invasive species in the United States. They swarm the nests of ground-dwelling lizards, eating vulnerable eggs, or even attacking and killing young lizards.

That’s where conservation efforts, like the one Williams works on with zoos across Texas, play an important role. The program releases nearly a thousand young lizards each year.

These hatchlings, which can easily fit in the palm of a hand, are packaged in individual Tupperware containers and then released in the desert scrub. Williams says that his graduate student, Kira Gangbin, has been working on a targeted poison to cut down fire ant numbers and help keep these hatchlings alive. These efforts will hopefully keep horned lizard populations thriving for many more years. Just remember: If you come across a horned lizard on a hike through the Texas desert, give it a wide berth, or risk a foul, bloody surprise.

#4604. Hotter Honda Civic Type R HRC Is ‘In Development’ for American Buyers

And the brand is using the SEMA Show to show off an electrified Baja Trophy Truck and a Prelude built for racing, too.

Honda still has not actually confirmed plans to sell a hotter Civic Type R with an HRC badge on it, but the Japanese brand has spent much of the past year hinting at just that. A concept has been shown off; development has been recorded in a YouTube video; and a window for a reveal shared by an executive has even come and gone.

The latest development, though, is the clearest sign yet of a coming retail product. Officially, Honda is confirming that the Civic Type R HRC Concept (seen above) is “in development for the U.S. market.”

Granted, that stops just short of a confirmation of plans to actually build it, but a statement of intent to develop a car for a specific market is the clear final step before announcing that said model will reach those shores as a production offering. Honda will also be bringing the concept to the 2026 SEMA Show in Las Vegas, so American buyers can get a first look at it next week.

While the concept has been shown off a few times, Honda still has not said exactly what is different between the HRC Type R and its more basic relative. The development video offered some hints on the aero side, showing off a new front bumper design along with a changed rear wing. Both the version shown initially and the slightly-less-camouflaged version shown in that video highlight what looks like some sort of winglet above the back of the flared front fenders, an aggressive element that could be the visual signature of the HRC variant.

In addition to the Type R HRC Concept, Honda is bringing a few other offerings to SEMA. One is the latest Passport trophy truck, set to be the first hybrid to ever enter the SCORE World Desert Championship. Honda is bringing a club racer based on the Prelude, too. This is a Hasport Performance build, replacing the transmission-free hybrid setup in the Prelude with both the 2.0-liter turbocharged I-4 engine and six-speed manual transmission from a Civic Type R. While this build is sure to appeal to Honda fans who want a Prelude Type R, it appears to be more a proof of concept for tuners than anything resembling a hint at a product that the brand insists is not in the pipeline any time soon.

#4603. Rivian’s electric van gets 30% more range and AWD, now delivering

Rivian has started delivering the first major hardware upgrade to its electric van since production began in 2021: a bigger LFP battery pack good for 30% more range, and a new dual-motor AWD version.

The company confirmed in its Q3 2026 shareholder presentation that deliveries of the new variants began in early October. That’s the first real spec bump for a van that has been stuck at about 160 miles of rated range for years.

Rivian first mentioned the upgrade in its Q4 2025 letter, which we covered in February when Amazon’s fleet of Rivian vans grew 50%. At the time, Rivian only said it was “developing” a larger battery and AWD to “expand EDV route coverage” in Amazon’s network.

Now it’s shipping. In today’s presentation, Rivian says the new variants are “specifically designed to expand route coverage into more rural networks,” with the AWD configuration and the bigger pack offering “a 30% increase in range.”

EPA certification documents for the 2027 EDV 700, issued September 17, list the new pack at 129 kWh usable. Rivian has marketed the current van with a 100 kWh LFP pack, so that’s roughly 29% more energy, which lines up with the 30% range claim.

The upgrade is limited to the bigger 700 van, the one with 652 cubic feet of cargo space. The smaller 500 keeps its existing pack and front-wheel drive.

The EPA filing gives unadjusted lab range figures, which always run high because they skip the correction for real-world driving:

Rivian rates the current 700 at “up to 160 miles.” Apply Rivian’s 30% to that and the new FWD van lands around 208 miles. Using the AWD van’s smaller 23% gain from the EPA tests, we estimate the dual-motor version at about 195 to 200 miles.

So AWD costs roughly a third of the range gain. For a van, that’s a fine trade. Rural routes mean longer distances between stops, plus gravel, mud, and snow, which is exactly where a front-wheel-drive van with a full load of packages in the back struggles.

200 miles is roughly what Rivian promised for the van when deliveries to Amazon started in 2022, before the rated figure settled closer to 160 miles. Rivian is finally there, four years later.

The timing helps on the sales side too. Rivian’s van business is still overwhelmingly Amazon, years after the exclusivity period ended in late 2023. We spotted a Rivian van in Walmart+ livery on a car hauler in Indiana just this week, though neither company has announced a deal.

The competition has also thinned out. GM ended BrightDrop van production in Ontario and Canoo went bankrupt, leaving Ford’s E-Transit as the main full-size electric alternative in the US.

Rivian needs to make the sales to USPS. I am starting to see those vans all the time now. It looks like it is designed from ground up to optimize for delivery. Extra height for drivers, lower floor of entry, great visibility in the front. Low bumper and lower headlight position for safety. Overall, great design.

Too bad that GM dropped Brightdrop van just as they are getting popular. I see a lot of FedEx trucks are now Bright drop. Perfect timing when diesel price is thru the roof. GM never have the long term view and always good at starting something but give up just before it becomes a hot seller.

This is the upgrade the van needed. 160 miles was always fine for dense urban Amazon routes, but it boxed Rivian out of a big chunk of the fleet market: rural delivery, utilities, telecom, anyone who can’t guarantee a short loop and an overnight charge.

Getting to around 200 miles real-world, with AWD as an option, opens a lot of those routes. And unlike most of the EV van market right now, Rivian is actually building and improving its product rather than killing it.

The question is whether Rivian can turn that into customers other than Amazon. A Walmart+ wrap on a car hauler is a nice sign. We’d want to see a real order. If you’re running a fleet and these specs change your math, we’d love to hear from you.

#4602. Fierce turtles square off in a rare woodland turf battle

Published Nov 1, 2026 10:10 AM EST

At first, it appears that two turtles with yellow spots are calmly sitting side by side. Suddenly, one of them turns, slowly—and lunges out with its head, its open beak clearly trying to take an aggressive chomp out of its neighbor. Moments later, the turtle tries again. Now, both reptiles are going head-to-head, though each is retracted into the protection of its shell.

The two combatants are male eastern box turtles (Terrapene carolina carolina) competing for dominance. Eastern box turtles are a subspecies of the common box turtle (Terrapene carolina), with bright orange and yellow coloring on its dark shell. They live throughout the eastern and midwestern United States.

“I wouldn’t say that they’re normally aggressive, but male box turtles can definitely become territorial, especially since males’ home ranges (the area they frequently occupy) often overlap,” Eamon Caffrey, the turtle research coordinator at Mass Audubon who captured the video, tells Popular Science. “We do occasionally see this sort of brawling behavior between two males when out in the field; you just have to get lucky enough to actually witness it. This experience was a first for me, and I was thrilled to capture it on camera.”

Over the summer, another Mass Audubon staff member saw two male box turtles opting for a pushing contest instead of biting. At one point, one of the two flipped the other contestant onto its back and pushed him down a small hill. Box turtle battles can also feature spinning each other around.

“From my understanding, fights between male box turtles are much more opportunistic than anything else,” Caffrey tells Popular Science. “Often, when two males come in contact, they will display a variety of aggressive behaviors that can include head butting, shell ramming, biting, pushing, and shoving – all in attempts to assert dominance. These disputes are often territorial but can be over mates as well.”

What’s more, the turtle with the darker shell is a well-known individual over 30 years old. Caffrey says he’s seen him various times this year, and since capturing the video the celebrity reptile has been spending time in an area where the Mass Audubon team frequently spot two to three adult females. However, there’s been no trace of his opponent.

“Does that mean he ‘won’ the battle?” Caffrey muses. “Who knows.”

#4601. Toyota's New ‘Woodland’ SEMA Concepts Prove Even Minivans Deserve to Go Off-Roading

The brand is reimagining its ‘Woodland’ trim level with five concepts that push the soft-road package to new levels, complete with matching liveries.

Toyota already showed us its vision for tackling snow-covered mountains with its Snowhunter concepts. Naturally, the carmaker chose its most rugged trucks and SUVs as the basis for these snow-conquering machines. But what about minivan owners, or people who drive electric crossovers? What happens when they want to venture off-road? Well, Toyota has something for them this year, too: its new Woodland concepts give the RAV4, Grand Highlander, Sienna, bZ EV, and Crown Signia their own off-road treatment.

Built for the 2026 SEMA Show, the five Woodland concepts give some of Toyota's more family-friendly models an off-road makeover. All five vehicles were developed with a common design theme, one established by the company’s CALTY Design Research branch: combining everything that makes these vehicles great for hauling the family, with an extra dose of adventure.

Each vehicle is finished in Horizon Blue paint. Toyota didn't select that color just because it thought it would look pretty; it's a nod to classic Toyota models from the 1960s, including the Stout, Crown, and Corona. Contrasting the lovely blue shade are black accents on the hoods and roofs, giving the vehicles a distinctive two-tone appearance.

But Toyota didn’t just give the vehicles a paint job and call it a day. The five concepts share several off-road upgrades, including suspension lift kits, oversized fender flares, rugged satin-black wheels wrapped in all-terrain tires, and roof racks with crossbars. That might not be enough to conquer the Rubicon Trail, but it certainly makes these family haulers look ready for something more adventurous than the morning school drop-off.

While all of the concepts are interesting, the most surprising might be the Toyota Sienna version, which goes above and beyond the previous Woodland variant. Minivans excel at taking the whole family to grandma's house or helping a friend move across town, but you don't often see one driving off into the woods. Give one some additional ground clearance and all-terrain tires, however, and suddenly it starts looking like a pretty compelling adventure vehicle.

And that's the point Toyota is making with these concepts. We already know the 4Runner can get you almost anywhere. But with a little help, even the more family-focused vehicles in Toyota's lineup might be capable of taking you considerably farther off the beaten path than you'd expect.

#4599. How to build an air purifier in 6 simple steps

Published Nov 1, 2026 3:00 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

Though invisible itself, the air we breathe is a microcosm of identifiable pollen, fungal spores, viruses, dust particles, and fine particles of human pollution from everything from cars to asphalt sidewalks. It’s not something we should obsess over day to day, but as more people measure air quality on their own, many are getting readings they’d prefer to address. However, not everyone wants to buy an air purifier, which can cost several hundred dollars.

One proposed solution for at-home air filtration is to use readily available materials like cardboard, box fans, square HVAC filters, and everyone’s favorite building material: duct tape. I did a version of this myself for PopSci, and, though I have mixed feelings about the process, I’m overall satisfied with the result. Here, we’ll go through what I built, how I built it, and my overall conclusions after using it, along with resources for anyone interested in reading further.

There are several configurations for making your own air purifier at home. One of the most documented is a Corsi-Rosenthal box, or CR box for short. It’s essentially an air filter cube, which is what I’ll be calling mine, with four sides made of furnace filters and one side made of a standard box fan (seen above). The fan pulls air through the filters and pushes out cleaner air than came in.

The United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) provides a lot of information about DIY air cleaners, including visual construction guides, tips on improving DIY air cleaners, and general air cleaner usage advice. EPA research on DIY air cleaners for wildfire smoke will also inevitably interest those in wildfire-prone areas who don’t want to purchase an air purifier for smoke.

These resources were used extensively throughout this project. Instead of using this guide as a total replacement for these resources, use this page as a waypoint for how an individual or student group might use one of these devices, with practical concerns highlighted along the way.

I went to my local Walmart and bought a Lasko box fan, two pairs of Filtrete 20-inch MERV 11 furnace filters, and a roll of Duck Brand General Purpose Masking Tape. This represents what a typical consumer might buy without specialty ordering options or bulk purchasing. The total came to $73.58 before taxes and $78.36 after Florida state sales tax.

The box fan, or any fan in a roughly square housing, should be a modern ETL- or UL-listed fan (clearly marked on the box) because older fans and those not ETL- or UL-listed may have issues when run facing upward. This is a safety issue and should not be skipped.

Since the cardboard box your fan comes in will likely become part of your air filter cube, it’s worth getting one that isn’t damaged, though you can tape over small tears.

EPA guidance recommends MERV13 or equivalent filters for the best experience. The MERV scale indicates how much and what kinds of particles the device can filter. High-tier MERV filters can be costly, so I opted for MERV11 since I was able to get a fairly good deal (around $23) per two-pack of these panels, and the notable difference between MERV11 and MERV13 was that the latter can handle forest fire smoke particles, which is not an issue in my area.

You can assemble your air filter cube in less than an hour, even with one person. Rather than a strict job that requires exhaustive measuring and cutting, it’s more of an approximate job that relies on the magic of tape to do the heavy lifting. This is a feasible parent-and-child project for those 6+ and a solo project for those 10+.

For this project, we want air to flow in through the filters and out through the fan. That means that the part of the fan that blows air out needs to be on the exterior of your cube, and the back side of the fan that pulls in air needs to be on the inside of your cube. Like a surgeon marking which limb to operate on before making the first cut, I marked the interior of my fan with ‘I’s for safety. Meanwhile, your filters should have arrows. Those arrows should point towards the inside of the cube.

Place two filters together and use a small piece of tape to connect them as shown. Remember to have the arrows pointing inwards. Continue taping the filters until you form a square. You can either use two people here or secure one filter vertically with a trash bin to do it solo.

The resulting square will be flimsy and contain cracks that air can get through. Tape the seams with duct tape. Don’t worry about being imperfect on the first try. In fact, going over the seams multiple times will only make your cube more secure and airtight.

At this point, your square of filters should be feeling more and more structurally sound. You can now flip it over and repeat the simple taping method from Step 2 on the side that was previously on the ground.

Remember, the box is an important part of the final product. If you place your square over the box, you’ll see they’re roughly the same size. Carefully cut out the most structurally sound side of the box and trim it to be roughly the size of your filter square. It won’t need to be perfect. I used scissors for this, as if imitating a school project, but a standard box cutter or multitool with a cutting edge would be better.

When done, tape the cardboard to one end of your filter square. Your air filter cube now has a bottom.

As a last step, take the fan and put it on the top side of the box, taping it down carefully. If your fan has rounded corners, tape those too. If you notice small gaps in the fan housing, you can seal them with tape, provided they aren’t ventilation openings or near electrical components.

At this point, you have a completed air filter cube. With the fan side up, plug it into an outlet and turn the fan on. Look for structural integrity, a smooth spinning blade with no obstructions from tape or cardboard, and no unusual sounds or vibrations. I recommend being around your new filter cube for a bit before leaving it unattended. Follow any fan manufacturer guidance about long-term or unattended usage.

While I opted not to, you may optionally wish to cover the top of your air filter cube with the cardboard from the other side of the fan box, cutting out a circular hole over the spot where the blades spin. This reduces unintended air recirculation and overall increases the efficiency of the box.

Verdict: Making an air filter cube or CR box is a worthwhile experiment that results in a usable final product, but it may not be the best bang for your buck out there.

After having run my air filter cube for several days now, despite not currently being in possession of an air quality monitor, I can still tell it has worked. For example, there is visible dust on the outside of the filters, which accumulated while I was cleaning dusty gear nearby. Furthermore, neither the grill nor the fan blades themselves are showing the dust that typically accumulates on long-running fans. I would call this project, from an engineering perspective, an obvious success.

Functional mechanics aren’t the only issue, though. Money is time and time is money, and both of these are major issues with these boxes.

One of my biggest complaints about how CR boxes are described to the public is that they are “marketed” as cheap when filters are so expensive. Claims of hyper-cheap CR boxes with EPA-like performance are abundant, though EPA sources use MERV13. My use of MERV11, while reasonable, is another reason to call my creation an air filter cube rather than a true CR box.

Low-cost air purifiers are available commercially that even include HEPA filtration. For example, the Dreo Air Purifier for Home is just $44 right now and, according to Google Chrome’s Shopping Insights tool, despite its $100 MSRP, has never been above $56.

The Dreo air purifier highlights a lot of what feels absent from a DIY air filter cube: a small body you can comfortably place in your home, quiet operation, and filter changes that don’t require completely rebuilding the air purifier every time the filters are used up. For average consumers, I suspect something like the Dreo, or even a larger air purifier like the Levoit Core 300, is going to be a much better option in nearly every way.

Where this really shines is student science. Building your own air filtration cube is fun, sort of like Minecraft block crafting in real life. Students can explore airflow, cost-effectiveness of different materials, and bring home a usable appliance at the end of a one-hour lesson.

I particularly like the idea of students experimenting with different MERV levels, or comparing the effectiveness of low-cost commercial purifiers to their air filtration cubes. Students can, and should, ask themselves at what point the additional health benefits stop justifying the costs in time and money. These sorts of questions are at the core of environmental and healthcare policies that dictate our real world.

#4598. Healthier Salt Substitute May Prevent Millions of Deaths From Heart Disease

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A simple swap for salt could spare millions of cardiovascular disease-related deaths, new research suggests.

In a study published in Nature Health on November 4, researchers at The George Institute for Global Health modeled the potential impact of 193 countries switching from regular table salt to potassium-enriched salt.

They found the switch could prevent nearly 3 million deaths and more than 10 million new cases of heart and kidney disease worldwide each year.

In the United States, this simple salt swap could prevent nearly 105,000 deaths and about 492,000 new cases a year, the researchers estimated.

About 130.6 million U.S. adults have cardiovascular disease, according to the American Heart Association (AHA).

Liping Huang, PhD, a senior data analyst in the Food Policy Division at The George Institute for Global Health and co-lead author of the study, told Healthline the team started with current blood pressure levels by sex, age, and country.

The researchers then estimated how replacing all salt with a salt substitute would change people’s sodium and potassium intake, blood pressure, and disease risk, she said.The team modeled a blend of 75% sodium chloride and 25% potassium chloride. The study estimated these yearly results worldwide:

The authors wrote that the model relied on data from a few years ago and on many assumptions, and that any large-scale switch would take years.

Potassium-enriched salt replaces some of the sodium chloride in regular table salt with potassium chloride, according to The George Institute.Asked where other salts like kosher salt and sea salt fit in, Huang said those salts may contain some trace elements “which has those health halos around them, but essentially they’re still primarily sodium chloride.”Huang noted that potassium-enriched salt tastes “about the same as a regular table salt.” She said it’s possible a small number of people with a sensitive palate could taste a difference.

Huang said that “it’s really hard for people to cut back their salt intake.”“But the easier way is just to replace part of the sodium chloride in our normal salt with potassium chloride, because increasing potassium intake also helps to reduce blood pressure,” she said.The two minerals play opposite roles in the body, according to Cheng-Han Chen, MD, a board certified interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA. Chen wasn’t involved in the study.

“While sodium causes water retention and increased blood pressure, potassium will help the kidneys remove sodium from the body and lower blood pressure,” Chen told Healthline.Huang said she worked on an earlier trial of about 21,000 people in 600 rural villages in northern China in 2021.

People who used potassium-enriched salt had a 14% lower risk of stroke, a 13% lower risk of cardiovascular events, and a 12% lower risk of early death than those who used regular salt, according to a 2021 study in The New England Journal of Medicine that summarized the trial’s results.

The World Health Organization (WHO) endorsed potassium-enriched salt in a 2025 guideline, saying it can reduce blood pressure and the risk of cardiovascular disease.

The AHA said potassium-based salt substitutes can help lower blood pressure in some adults. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued labeling guidance in 2020 allowing an alternate name for potassium chloride on ingredient labels to include the word “salt.”“We think that blood pressure begins to improve as soon as 1 week after cutting back on sodium intake. The full benefit typically takes up to 4 weeks,” Chen said.

“We generally recommend a daily sodium limit of 2,300 milligrams (mg), ideally under 1,500 mg a day. Most people consume over 3,000 mg of sodium a day, well above the recommended limit,” Chen said.The WHO recommends less than 2,000 mg of sodium per day and suggests at least 3,510 mg of potassium a day.In the United States, more than 70% of salt intake comes from processed and restaurant foods, according to the AHA.

Huang said that some people with advanced chronic kidney disease should avoid potassium-enriched salt.When the kidneys don’t work well, the body may not clear extra potassium efficiently, she said. That can lead to hyperkalemia, or high potassium levels in the blood, which can raise the risk of cardiac arrest, Huang said.Among people with stage 3 to stage 5 kidney disease, switching to salt substitutes could prevent about 750,000 deaths a year by lowering blood pressure and cause about 100,000 deaths a year from hyperkalemia, the researchers estimated.The AHA said that people with kidney disease or who take medications that affect potassium should check with a healthcare professional before using these products.

An estimated 37 million U.S. adults have chronic kidney disease, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Potassium-enriched salt is available at supermarkets in the U.S. Many major U.S. grocery chains, including Kroger, Walmart, and Publix, carry two types of products, according to their websites:

Potassium-enriched salt typically costs about twice as much as regular salt, according to the study.Huang said she hoped people would see the results and start thinking of the switch as “a simple thing I can do for their own health.”
