#4597. 2026 Gifts of the Year: Our editors have picked the best presents for anyone on your list

Updated Nov 1, 2026 3:42 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

A gift card isn’t a terrible present, but we believe you can do better. That’s why the editors here at Popular Science have put together this list of our favorite gifts of the year. We spend all year researching, testing, and covering products, so we know what we’re talking about. Even if you don’t end up grabbing one of these exact products, it’s a great place to start. Show them you know what they like and leave the gift cards for your nephew who you don’t really like that much.

Popular Science‘s sibling brands have also selected unique products for their own Gift of the Year awards. See their best-in-class gift selections for this holiday season at PCMag, CNET, Mashable, Lifehacker, and ZDNET.

Waterproof trail shoes usually look and feel too bulky and—let’s be honest—kind of nerdy. The Speedgoat 7 GTX keeps the regular Speedgoat 7’s supercritical EVA midsole and Vibram Megagrip outsole, then wraps them in a GORE-TEX Invisible Fit membrane and a recycled Cordura upper. It’s a lot of technical materials, but they’re wrapped in a design that actually looks cool with a pair of jeans. Toggle laces work with gloves on, there’s a loop for attaching gaiters (sold separately), and reflective details run all the way around for dark November runs. We recommend going up a half-size from your giftee’s typical number for a better fit.

This little device gives the gift of time that would otherwise be spent doomscrolling. Phone screen-time limits are easy to dismiss because the override button sits right under your thumb. Brick moves the override into another room. The $59 block has no battery, just an NFC chip. You pick the apps to lock in the free iPhone or Android app, tap your phone to the Brick, and those apps stay locked until you walk back and tap again. One Brick works with multiple phones, so a household can share it, and the app includes five emergency unlocks per device for real emergencies. It requires iOS 18 or Android 12 and later. Brick is also HSA and FSA eligible, which makes it a stocking stuffer you can buy with pretax money.

Insta360 made its name with 360-degree and action cameras, and the Luna Ultra is its first pocket gimbal camera, co-engineered with Leica. The main camera pairs a Leica Summicron lens with a 1-inch sensor that records up to 8K at 30fps, and a second telephoto camera on a 1/1.3-inch sensor handles zoomed shots and background blur. A three-axis gimbal keeps footage steady while you walk. The 2-inch OLED touchscreen pops off and works as a wireless monitor and remote, so you can frame a shot of yourself from across the room. It’s a serious content creation tool that’s fun to use, which is a rarity.

You don’t need a massive backyard to have a true outdoor pizza oven. The propane cooker weighs 26.4 pounds and measures 16.9 inches wide, yet Gozney rates it to reach 950 degrees Fahrenheit, which is more than enough to put a perfect char on a true Neopolitan style pie. Gozney’s lateral rolling flame wraps heat over the top of the pizza while a 12mm stone floor stores heat for the crust. An infrared thermometer makes a smart add-on gift, since the oven won’t tell you when the stone is ready. You’ll selfishly also probably get some free pizza out of it.

A 65-inch black rectangle is a lot of nothing to stare at when the TV is off. LG’s Gallery TV LX7B fills that space with art. The 4K Mini LED set has a matte screen that cuts reflections and a snow-white magnetic frame that snaps onto the bezel, and when it’s idle it can display pieces from LG Gallery+, a library of more than 5,000 works (some features require a Gallery+ subscription). It runs webOS 26 with Google Gemini built in. Whether the receiver is a film buff or a die-hard design enthusiast, this TV fits the bill.

This is a product we use every single day. The Theragun Mini Plus is Therabody’s smallest heated massage gun, and its attachment warms up to 131 degrees Fahrenheit across three heat levels. It has three speeds, two buttons, USB-C charging, and a travel lock that keeps it from switching on inside a gym bag. Therabody says heat plus percussion works three times faster than percussion alone, based on its own lab testing. You can run either therapy by itself, too. Don’t think this is only for hardcore gym rats. It’s great for people who just want to relax of even improve their sleep.

If you know a budding streamer or podcaster, this is a gift that grows with them. The Razer Seiren V3 Pro has both USB-C and XLR outputs, so it plugs straight into a PC now and into a mixer later when they upgrade their setup. It’s a dynamic mic with a 30mm cardioid capsule, a type that picks up less of a noisy room than most condensers. Onboard processing runs AI noise removal, a compressor, and a limiter on the mic itself, and Windows users can record 32-bit float audio through Razer Synapse. A tap-to-mute button, an RGB ring that shows mute and gain status, and an adjustable desk arm all come in the box.

The nightstand device, built for kids roughly 4 to 10, walks one child through morning, after-school, and bedtime routines a step at a time with visual prompts that work for kids who can’t read yet. It also handles alarm clock, sound machine, nightlight, and OK-to-wake duty. It has no camera or microphone, and kids can’t browse the web or download apps on it. Skylight sells it for $139.99, and the optional $39-per-year Buddy Plus plan adds rewards, timers, and read-aloud messages.

Fast wireless charging makes a magnetic battery pack hot, and heat makes phones slow their charging down. Anker’s fix in the MagGo 2 Pro is a tiny fan. The 10,000mAh pack charges at up to 25W over Qi2.2, and Anker says the fan keeps its back under about 97 degrees Fahrenheit while it works. Anker rates it to take an iPhone 17 Pro to 50 percent in about 25 minutes. A screen shows battery level and charging speed, a built-in stand props the phone up for in-flight movies, and the USB-C port refills the pack at 45W. It costs $109.99. Older phones, including the iPhone 15 Pro, top out at 15W.

Google hadn’t released a new standalone smart speaker since the Nest Audio in 2020. The Google Home Speaker is built around Gemini for Home instead of the old Assistant, so you can stack several requests into one sentence or correct yourself mid-command. It plays 360-degree sound from a 58mm driver, two of them pair with a Google TV Streamer for surround sound, and it doubles as a Thread border router and Matter hub. It costs $99.99 and includes six months of Google Home Premium, which adds Gemini Live and continued conversation. After the trial, Premium runs $10 per month.

A $20 smart plug makes a surprisingly good energy audit. The Shelly Plug Gen4 measures real-time power draw from whatever is plugged into it, so you can see how much that garage fridge or space heater actually pulls. It connects over Matter, Wi-Fi, or Zigbee, works with Apple Home, Google Home, Alexa, SmartThings, and Home Assistant, and can run locally without touching the cloud. It handles loads up to 1,800 watts, with cutoffs for overheating, overcurrent, and voltage problems. Its built-in LED can change color to reflect current energy use. It costs $19.99 in black or white.

If you know someone constantly struggling to make work from the road work, the Sennheiser MOMENTUM 5 Wireless headphones are an audio oasis they will appreciate for years to come. The hybrid noise cancellation, 8-band graphic EQ, Snapdragon Sound, and other personalization features cut the noise and sculpt the sound, perfect for open-office escapees and in-control commuters. And a long-haul battery life delivers up to 57 hours of runtime, so playlists won’t run out somewhere over the Atlantic. Plus, the battery is user-replaceable, reducing e-waste and extending ownership. This is the perfect gift for music-loving control freqs.

Sonos isn’t the only way to fill a house with speakers that talk to each other. Denon’s redesigned Home lineup runs on HEOS, which can link up to 64 speakers across a home, and the three sizes scale with the room. The $399 Home 200 plays stereo from three tweeters and a 4-inch woofer. The $599 Home 400 adds two upward-firing drivers for Dolby Atmos Music, and the $799 Home 600 packs eight drivers, including dual 6.5-inch woofers, each with its own amplifier. All three take Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, USB-C, and aux. The stone and charcoal finishes look more like something from a furniture store than an electronics aisle.

The Bose LifeStyle Ultra Home Theater Set is perfect for homes that struggle with the volume of content and components. From the soundbar to the wireless satellites and subwoofer, everything is compact and design-conscious, perfect for a minimalist who doesn’t want to sacrifice expression. Bose SpeechClarity uses AI enhancement to make dialogue more audible without having to ride the volume constantly. CustomTune calibrates immersion to the room’s actual acoustics. And when it’s not movie night, stream music via AirPlay 2/Google Cast, no app required. Add more speakers later for a multiroom setup, making this a great gift for someone who wants to scale up a whole-home setup without sacrificing space.

#4596. GM to Pay $220 Million in Settlement After Alleged Privacy Violations

General Motors was reportedly selling millions of drivers’ data to insurance companies. Now, the company will fork over millions to 35 states and the District of Columbia.

General Motors is set to pay $220 million in a settlement with the attorneys general of 35 states and the District of Columbia after claims that the automaker sold drivers’ location and behavior data to brokers without permission.

GM’s Smart Driver program sits at the heart of the settlement. The driver monitoring system was meant to log driving data to help monitor driving habits, and was active between 2016 and 2024. However, the program regularly logged hard braking and speeding events, which GM then sold to data brokers under contracts that were used for insurance products, the group of attorneys general claims.

“The coalition’s investigation found that in reality, GM sold this information to data brokers under contracts that specified the data was to be used for insurance products. The data brokers sold the data to insurance companies, who could then change the drivers’ premiums based on their driving habits. GM did not disclose to drivers that their data would be sold for this purpose,” a statement from New York attorney general Letitia James reads.

“Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it’s protected, and the choices customers have about what they share,” a GM spokesperson said to Reuters.

Over 370,000 drivers enrolled in Smart Driver weren’t even aware that the program was tracking their driving, the attorneys general claim. The OnStar app apparently said that they were not enrolled in Smart Driver before GM quietly un-enrolled them without notification. One driver even reportedly faced a 22 percent increase in insurance premiums because of “personal driving information provided by a data broker.”

Many customers signed up for Smart Driver at dealerships when purchasing a new vehicle; GM offered OnStar and Smart Driver as a one-step package deal to customers buying new vehicles, with heavy incentives for dealerships to increase sign-up rates. New York AG James claims that GM offered bonuses based in part on how many customers they signed up for GM’s connected vehicle services, including Smart Driver, and even ranked dealerships based on their enrollment numbers.

“People bought a car, not a tracking device,” as Oregon attorney general Dan Rayfield put it in a statement.

Settlement money will be doled out to consumers in Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Hawai’i, Idaho, Illinois, Kansas, Kentucky, Maine, Massachusetts, Maryland, Michigan, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia. GM previously paid $12.75 million to settle a California investigation into an alleged sale of drive data to brokers.

A New York transplant hailing from the Pacific Northwest, Emmet White has a passion for anything that goes: cars, bicycles, planes, and motorcycles. After learning to ride at 17, Emmet worked in the motorcycle industry before joining Autoweek in 2022 and Road & Track in 2024. The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

#4595. Energy Drinks, Stimulant Supplements Linked to Higher Heart Risks in Young Adults

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Your hub for heart health management, insights, and solutions

Learn the basics to keeping your heart healthy

New research suggests that caffeinated energy drinks and stimulant supplements are associated with significantly higher risks of serious heart problems, including cardiac arrest and heart attack in young adults.

The findings, to be presented at the American Heart Association (AHA) Scientific Sessions 2026 November 6–9 in Chicago, are preliminary and can’t prove that energy drinks cause heart problems.

Still, the results highlight concerning cardiovascular effects of these popular products, particularly among adults under 35 who consume them regularly.

“These products are marketed as everyday pick-me-ups and sold next to soda and bottled water, so most people assume they carry no real risk,” study author Sai Samayamanthula, a fourth-year medical student at the University of Virginia School of Medicine in Charlottesville, VA, said in a news release.

“For many healthy people, if these products are consumed occasionally, the risk is probably small. However, individuals who consume energy drinks or other stimulant-containing supplements regularly can quickly exceed the recommended daily limit for caffeine, so it’s important for people to know that there may be a risk of cardiovascular harm with these products,” Samayamanthula continued.

Researchers from the University of Virginia School of Medicine analyzed 28,345 reports submitted to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) between 2017 and 2025.

Of these, 854 involved caffeinated energy drinks or stimulant supplements, while the remaining reports involved non-stimulant products.

Compared with non-stimulant products, cardiac arrest was reported approximately 11 times more often with energy drinks and stimulant supplements. Heart attacks were reported 4.5 times more often, while ventricular arrhythmias and palpitations were reported about four times more frequently.

Nearly 45% of heart-related reports involved adults ages 18 to 34.

“Our findings support the case for more systematic safety monitoring of caffeine- and stimulant-containing products. In addition, healthcare professionals should remember to ask their younger patients who have palpitations, chest pain or fainting spells if they recently or regularly consume these products,” Samayamanthula said.

Gregory M. Marcus, MD, professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine, and chair of the 2026 AHA scientific statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease, wasn’t involved in the study, but said the research “raises concerns that products with very high amounts of caffeine may be harmful to the cardiovascular system.”

“Although there are biological reasons why that connection could be possible, the study does not prove that caffeine products cause these events, because other factors may have influenced the results found in this analysis,” Marcus said in a news release.

“More research is needed to understand whether these stimulant products are truly responsible for the reported heart-related events.”

Cheng-Han Chen, MD, board certified interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA, said the findings, although concerning, are not surprising. Chen wasn’t involved in the study.

“We know that energy drinks can have significant effects on the cardiovascular system, primarily because of their stimulant properties,” he told Healthline.

“Caffeine can increase blood pressure and heart rate, while other ingredients, such as guarana and taurine, may further contribute to cardiovascular stimulation and increased stress hormone levels. What is particularly concerning is the potential for these products to trigger serious complications, including abnormal heart rhythms, especially in people with underlying cardiovascular conditions.”

Chen agreed that occasional energy drink consumption is unlikely to have long-term consequences for heart health in most healthy individuals. However, he said that “frequent or excessive consumption can potentially increase the risk of hypertension and cardiac arrhythmias.”

An AHA scientific statement published in July 2026 notes that up to 400 milligrams of caffeine daily is generally considered safe for most healthy adults. That’s roughly equivalent to four or five 8-ounce cups of brewed coffee, depending on how it’s prepared.

However, some energy drinks contain up to three times as much caffeine per fluid ounce as brewed coffee.

Certain energy drinks may also contain stimulants, such as guarana, yerba mate, theobromine, synephrine, and yohimbine.

These ingredients may compound caffeine’s effects on the cardiovascular system.

“Caffeine stimulates the cardiovascular system, primarily by increasing sympathetic nervous system activity. This can cause the heart to beat faster, raise blood pressure, and increase the workload on the heart,” Chen said.

“Energy drinks may contain additional stimulants, such as guarana and taurine, which can further increase blood pressure and stress hormone levels. With excessive consumption, these effects can become more pronounced and potentially interfere with the heart’s normal electrical activity, increasing the risk of abnormal heart rhythms. People with underlying cardiovascular conditions, particularly hypertension or a predisposition to arrhythmias, may be especially vulnerable to these effects.”

Other research has echoed these concerns. A 2025 review suggests that high-volume energy drink consumption can prolong the heart’s QTc interval, increase blood pressure, and raise heart rate beyond the effects of caffeine alone.

“There is growing concern about the cardiovascular effects of energy drinks and stimulant-containing supplements, particularly among younger adults,” Chen said.

“One challenge is that younger individuals may not recognize that these products can have significant effects on their heart and blood pressure, especially when consumed frequently or in combination with other caffeinated products.”

Young adults accounted for a substantial portion of the FDA reports included in the study, highlighting potential cardiovascular concerns for this age group.

People with existing heart conditions, a history of irregular heart rhythms, or heightened caffeine sensitivity may face additional risks. Those with undiagnosed genetic heart conditions may also be vulnerable.

A 2024 study identified cases of sudden cardiac arrest occurring shortly after energy drink consumption, particularly among people with underlying inherited heart conditions.

“As a cardiologist, I am particularly concerned about people who may have underlying cardiovascular conditions that have not yet been diagnosed,” Chen said.

“Excessive stimulant intake can potentially trigger symptoms such as palpitations, chest discomfort, and lightheadedness. In susceptible individuals, it may also increase the risk of more serious complications, including abnormal heart rhythms.”

Additionally, combining energy drinks with strenuous exercise or alcohol may introduce additional cardiovascular risks.

The findings suggest an association between energy drinks, stimulant supplements, and reported cardiovascular events, but they are preliminary and do not establish cause and effect.

The FDA database also relied on voluntary adverse-event reports, meaning some events may never be reported, while others may receive disproportionate attention.

Researchers also do not yet know how many people consumed these products without experiencing any problems. Without this variable, the reports cannot establish actual risk.

Other factors, including underlying health conditions, medications, and lifestyle habits, may also influence the results. More systematic research and controlled clinical trials are needed.

For most healthy adults, consuming up to 400 milligrams of caffeine per day is generally considered safe.

However, Chen noted that individual tolerance for caffeine may vary, and people with underlying cardiovascular conditions, particularly high blood pressure or abnormal heart rhythms, may need to limit or avoid caffeine altogether.

“Energy drinks can vary considerably in their caffeine content and serving sizes,” Chen said.

“Depending on the product, a single can may contain anywhere from 80 to 300 milligrams of caffeine. This means that consuming even one or two energy drinks can put someone close to or above the recommended daily limit, particularly when combined with coffee, tea, or other caffeinated supplements.”

Seek emergency medical attention if you experience chest pain, particularly if it’s accompanied by shortness of breath, fainting, or other symptoms of a possible heart attack.

If you live with a heart condition, ask your doctor about your daily caffeine intake to determine whether you need to cut back.

According to Chen, warning signs of excessive stimulant intake may include:

“Depending on the severity of these symptoms, medical attention may be necessary,” he said.

Still, most people may not need to give up caffeine entirely. Monitoring your habits could help protect your heart health. This may include:

“I encourage people to read product labels carefully and be aware of their total daily caffeine consumption,” Chen said. “I particularly recommend that people with underlying cardiovascular conditions avoid energy drinks.”

#4594. The grossest thing you touch every day, according to science

Published Nov 1, 2026 5:02 PM EST

It’s probably not something you want to think about, but what do you think is the dirtiest thing you touch every day? If you commute via subway, you might suspect a stairwell handle or train pole as the most likely culprit. If you go from your house to your car to an office, maybe it’s the elevator button or the key fob you have to dig out of your bag. All very good guesses–you might even be tempted to pull out your phone and look up the correct answer.

“It might surprise people, but the dirtiest thing they encounter every day is their own cellphone,” says Caitlin Mangan, a Lab Manager for Gillson Sciences. “People take them everywhere with them, including the bathroom. They are touched thousands of times a day, without people cleaning them or washing their hands in between tasks.”

The University of Michigan’s Institute for Healthcare Policy & Innovation puts it this way: Your cellphone is 10 times dirtier than a toilet seat. Yeah, that’s pretty gross.

The frequency of contact contributes to that grossness. The study shows that, on average, people check their phones 47 times a day. And like your clothing and shoes, you carry your beloved phone through various environments of differing cleanliness levels. In fact, that subway pole may actually be cleaner than your iPhone.

“It depends on how often the areas are cleaned,” says Mangan. “For example, an office building door handle typically has less people touching it day-to-day, but because of that it might not be cleaned as frequently and therefore has a high risk of having germs. Whereas a subway pole that is cleaned daily and properly sanitized will have less germs to transfer.”

Cellphones have been known to carry skin bacteria like Staphylococcus and Streptococcus, as well as fecal bacteria like E. coli and Enterococcus faecalis. These bacteria can cause skin infections, strep throat, or gastrointestinal illnesses producing nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. You can help yourself by avoiding using your phone in the restroom, not placing it down on surfaces where germs likely lurk, and when speaking into it, not letting it touch your cheek or mouth.

Of course, you should also clean your phone with paper towels, alcohol, and cotton swabs whenever possible and follow the number one rule of germ spread prevention: Wash your hands frequently and thoroughly.

#4593. VW Suspends ID.Golf EV Development Amid Financial Pressures: Report

The electric Golf is apparently being put on the shelf, at least for now.

It was only a few months ago that Volkswagen was showing teasers of the next-gen electric Golf to folks behind closed doors, but a new report now claims development on said vehicle is suspended until further notice—a development pause that is one of the many cuts being made by the Volkswagen Group as it looks to save cash amid financial pressures.

The hatchback, which was exxpected to be named ID.Golf, was meant to be the electric successor to the ID.3. Reuters reports that it viewed a memo written by CEO Thomas Schaefer that revealed the delay. "I know what the Golf means for Volkswagen and for Wolfsburg. That's why this decision was really not an easy one for us," the internal memo reportedly said. “We simply can't afford this work right now.”

Whether or not Volkswagen would sell the supposed ID.Golf in the U.S. remains a question. We haven’t seen a standard Golf on sale here since the introduction of the current Mk.8 generation; the GTI and Golf R performance variants live on, thankfully, but an electric version sure would open the discussion back up to bringing the mainstream version to American shores again.

But the news is a large blow to those in Europe who might’ve been expecting a successor to the ID.3 before the end of the decade. VW recently revealed the ID.3 Neo (above) that brought sweeping changes to the car, at least ensuring there will be an electric, Golf-like car on sale across the Pond for some time. Still, the jump to the ID.Golf is meant to be a large one, as VW planned the new model along with a transition to a new Scalable Systems Platform (SSP) architecture.

The caveat to this news is that VW is expressing this as simply a delay in development. That means the company is still planning on picking things up at a later date, so presumably, an ID.Golf is still in the product roadmap. We just don’t know when it could arrive.

#4592. Someone ran Rivian’s pedal-by-wire e-bike out of battery and things got weird

The ALSO TM-B is one of the most technologically interesting new e-bikes to hit the road in years, largely because it does away with one of the most fundamental parts of a bicycle: the mechanical connection between the pedals and rear wheel. With only copper wires connecting the pedals to the rear wheel, the TM-B is one of the most revolutionary new e-bikes in years.

But that raises an obvious question. What happens when the battery dies?

One early Launch Edition owner, Aaron Draczynski, decided to find out by deliberately running his TM-B down toward empty to see whether ALSO’s drive-by-wire system would leave him stranded.

He shared the experience on YouTube, discovering that the answer is surprisingly complicated – and involves something called “Infinite Turtle Mode.”

Unlike a conventional e-bike, where the rider’s pedaling mechanically turns the rear wheel through a chain or belt, the ALSO TM-B uses a pedal-by-wire drivetrain. Pedaling generates electricity, while the rear wheel is driven electrically.

That arrangement enables all sorts of interesting features, including electronically simulated gearing and the Launch Edition’s massive Level 10 boost mode, which can multiply rider input by up to 10 times.

But it also means there’s no traditional drivetrain to fall back on when the battery runs out.

Fortunately, the bike doesn’t simply go from full power to dead.

The owner began his experiment at 31% charge and quickly watched the bike progressively restrict its maximum assist as the battery drained closer to empty. From 23% to 13%, the maximum boost dropped from Level 8 to Level 5 as it began conserving battery.

By 10% charge, the bike was limited to Level 4. At 8%, it dropped to Level 3, followed by Level 2 at 5%. Shortly afterward, only Level 1 remained. Then at 4% battery, conventional electric assistance disappeared entirely.

Interestingly, the normal electronic shifting of the bike’s simulated software gears continued to work through most of that process. But when the battery reached 4%, things changed as the bike started exhibiting issues. The first sign of trouble came when the bike began seemingly randomly shifting gears while in manual mode without the rider even touching the shifter. Several times per second, the bike seemed to want to shift itself between gears.

Keep in mind that the TM-B doesn’t have actual physical gears (and no chain or derailleur, for that matter), but instead simulates various gears using predefined software to make the rider feel like they are working more or less intensely to pedal the bike.

Once the TM-B reached its final low-battery state, an infinity symbol appeared on the display and the bike entered what the owner referred to as “Infinite Turtle Mode.”

Instead of using stored battery energy to provide meaningful assistance, the system effectively attempts to pass the rider’s pedaling energy through the electronic drivetrain to keep the rear wheel turning. It’s similar in concept to those old crank-powered flashlights, which, even with a dead storage battery, would still illuminate for as long as the owner cranked them.

And on flat ground, the owner reported that the infinite turtle mode apparently worked surprisingly well.

Draczynski described the experience as roughly equivalent to pedaling a normal bicycle in fourth gear. There was resistance at the pedals, and he could maintain a reasonable pace without feeling like he was simply spinning his legs uselessly.

Then he reached a hill and found the limitation of that effectiveness. Even a slight incline transformed the experience, with the bike feeling more like it was permanently stuck in seventh or eighth gear. Getting home through his hilly neighborhood became, in his words, a “truly grueling ordeal.”

Manual shifting was also disabled in this mode, meaning there was no way to electronically select an easier virtual gear for climbing, since again, there aren’t any physical gears in the bike. Everything in the pedaling experience is software-simulated.

That’s an important limitation for a bike relying entirely on a drive-by-wire drivetrain. The infinite turtle mode might keep you moving with significant effort on level terrain, but it doesn’t turn a dead TM-B into a conventional bicycle, unless that conventional bicycle is being ridden through beach sand.

The low-power state apparently shuts down some other features as well. The owner could no longer lock or unlock the TM-B through ALSO’s smartphone app, though he did report the bike’s touchscreen controls continued working, and he guessed that the bike had shut down connectivity to conserve power for its key systems to operate.

Perhaps more concerning than the low-battery riding experience was what happened when this particular TM-B was simply sitting in the owner’s garage.

Describing another scenario he encountered, Draczynski says he left the bike sitting unplugged in his garage at around 70% charge. The following evening, it had fallen to 40%, and a day later it was down to 18%.

When he returned the next morning, the TM-B displayed a “Bike issue detected” message followed by “Install battery to ride.”

There was just one problem: the battery was already installed.

Plugging in the charger didn’t initially help because the bike apparently couldn’t detect its own battery, and thus charging didn’t begin. Worse, the battery refused to eject using the normal ejection process, leaving the owner unable to remove it and charge it off of the bike.

Ultimately, Draczynski used the physical reset button underneath the frame, which brought the system back to life. The bike recognized the battery again and began charging normally.

Much like modern EVs, I would imagine a lot of these issues will be fixed via a software update. Early adoption is fun but you’re basically beta testing a product for the company at full price.

That degree of overnight battery drain obviously isn’t something we’d expect from a normal e-bike, so hopefully this was either an isolated software issue or something ALSO can address with an update. For his part, Draczynski suspects that the bike might be draining its battery so heavily at rest due to the lack of a cell signal in his garage. “I was quite surprised at the drop from day to day,” he explained on Reddit. “If I had to wager a guess, the bike might be searching for a cellular signal, but there’s no reception in my garage so it’s just draining the battery.”

But the experiment offers an interesting first real-world look at one of the biggest questions surrounding ALSO’s unusual drivetrain.

A normal e-bike with a dead battery becomes a heavy bicycle. The TM-B instead becomes something much stranger: an electricity-generating exercise machine that uses your legs to generate current, electronically sends that current through the bike, and then uses it to turn the rear wheel.

And based on this testing, it does in fact work. Just try not to be at the bottom of a hill when you find out for yourself.

#4591. Bald eagle mistaken for trashbag on the road to recovery

Published Nov 2, 2026 9:00 AM EST

A Pennsylvania resident recently arrived home to find what looked like an unassuming black trash bag in their yard. But the bag moved and lifted its head. Turns out, it was not a bag, but a bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus). And something was very wrong with her.

A state Game Warden brought the eagle to Raven Ridge Wildlife Center in southern Pennsylvania to be checked out. The bird couldn’t stand and her legs were limp, which is a typical symptom of spinal trauma. Nonetheless, the team also tested the eagle for lead poisoning, and found that she indeed had lead in her system. Even though the eagle wasn’t showing signs of such poisoning, they weren’t surprised by these results.

In a 2022 study published in the journal Science, researchers investigated lead exposure in 1,210 bald and golden eagles (Aquila chrysaetos) in North America and found chronic lead poisoning in 46 to 47 percent of both eagles and acute lead poisoning in 27 to 33 percent of bald eagles. Lead exposure in eagles and other avian scavengers mostly occurs when they consume the remains of animals shot with lead ammunition and left behind by hunters.

“Lead poisoning is so common that even eagles brought in for other injuries are now routinely tested for it, and almost all show some level of lead in their system,” Tracie Young, Raven Ridge Wildlife Center director, tells Popular Science.

Even small quantities of lead can be extremely toxic. Lead poisoning can cause brain swelling, trouble breathing, weak muscles, dehydration, starvation, kidney and liver problems, or seizures, Young explains.

“Nerve damage can cause them to lose vision, coordination, and normal movement, so the bird may look ‘drunk’ or not be able to stand,” she continues. “When these eagles are starving, they lose their hunting skills and can’t catch food. As scavengers, they look for roadkill, but because they are uncoordinated, they often get hit by vehicles.”

It’s likely that this is what happened to the trash-bag-looking female eagle in Pennsylvania. At the wildlife center, she received chelation therapy for the lead poisoning. Chelation therapy involves the administration of administering specialized chemical agents that attach to the lead molecules in the bird’s blood and form a compound that is expelled, mostly via urine. The eagle also received physical therapy to regain strength in her legs and mitigate spinal pain and swelling.

Her rehabilitation process has been challenging, but not without its rewards. She is currently able to stand and lives in an outdoor area with an open space where she can continue her rehabilitation process. The eagle is a good candidate for release, but Young says she will require weeks of flight training.

“We urge all hunters and anglers to make a crucial choice: opt for lead-free ammunition and lead-free fishing gear,” the wildlife center wrote in a Facebook post. “This single decision at checkout can significantly improve the lives of countless eagles and other wildlife suffering from lead poisoning.”

#4589. 20 Best Chronographs for Drivers

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

These chronographs bring together mechanical ingenuity, motorsport heritage, and distinctive design, in a range of price points.

This article was updated in October 2026.

Few watch complications have as much character as the chronograph. Originally developed as a tool for measuring elapsed time, chronos became an essential piece of equipment in aviation, motorsport, and professional timing.

Today, the chronograph remains one of watchmaking’s most recognizable designs, with twin pushers, layered subdials, and tachymeter scales giving even a simple wristwatch a distinctly technical look. It’s also one of the few complications where the mechanical function is just as satisfying to operate as it is to look at.

For anyone getting into watches, chronographs offer an especially interesting entry point. The category spans everything from affordable Japanese quartz movements to sophisticated Swiss automatics, with plenty of variation in case architecture, dial layout, and movement design along the way.

There’s a lot to learn too, such as the difference between a standard chronograph and a flyback, the appeal of a column-wheel movement, or why certain vintage racing references have become so collectible. You can spend a little or a lot and still come away with a watch that has a story behind it.

We put together this selection with both new buyers and seasoned enthusiasts in mind. Some are modern interpretations of historically important designs, others have direct ties to motorsport, and a few offer interesting movements or complications that make them stand out from the usual three-hand watch.

💡 Expert Tip: Mechanical chronographs have more moving parts than standard watches, making routine servicing especially important. Plan on a professional service every five to seven years, and avoid operating the pushers underwater unless the watch is specifically designed for it.

The Omega Speedmaster features a stainless-steel case and bracelet with a fixed bezel and black aluminum ring displaying tachymeter markings. The 40mm round case houses a gray analog dial with luminescent silver-tone hands, index hour markers, and numeral minute markers at 5-minute intervals. The timepiece offers a date display and three chronograph subdials for 60 seconds, 30 minutes, and 12 hours. Powered by an Omega calibre 3330 automatic movement with a 52-hour power reserve, it has a scratch-resistant sapphire crystal and a pull/push crown.

The Seiko SSB479P1 features a 38.7mm stainless-steel case and bracelet and a Hardlex crystal. Its dial features luminous hands and index hour markers, a small seconds subdial, a 24-hour indicator, and a date display. Powered by Seiko’s 8T63 quartz movement, the chronograph measures elapsed time up to 60 minutes in one-fifth-second increments. A fixed tachymeter scale provides a way to calculate average speed, while 50-meter water resistance makes the watch suitable for everyday use.

Seiko has long been a gateway brand for watch enthusiasts, and this model offers a relatively affordable way to get a well-executed Japanese chronograph. Its sub-40mm case is also a welcome change from the oversize sports watches that have dominated much of the category.

The Fossil Signature CS-1 Master Calendar Chronoquartz features a 42mm stainless-steel case with a domed sapphire crystal and a dial designed to combine chronograph timing with calendar functions. Its layout includes day and month apertures, a central date hand that tracks the date around the outer chapter ring, and recessed subdials for the chronograph. Power comes from the Swiss Ronda 5040.F quartz movement, which drives the chronograph and triple-calendar display. The watch is available with a stainless-steel bracelet or an Italian leather strap, depending on the reference, and offers 50-meter water resistance. Its record-inspired dial texture and carefully arranged displays give it a more technical look than a conventional dress chronograph.

For someone just getting into watches, the combination of chronograph and full calendar complications offers plenty to explore, while its unconventional layout gives it a little more personality than a typical entry-level fashion watch.

The Hamilton American Classic Intra-Matic Chronograph features a 40mm stainless-steel case with a vintage-inspired profile and a contrasting two-register dial. Luminous hands and markers provide visibility, while a tachymeter scale adds a motorsport-inspired touch. The automatic version is powered by Hamilton’s H-31 movement, with a 60-hour power reserve, while the hand-wound Intra-Matic Chronograph H uses the H-51 caliber with the same power reserve. Both feature a sapphire crystal with antireflective coating and 100-meter water resistance.

Hamilton’s connection to American watchmaking and the Intra-Matic’s clear inspiration from its historic chronographs give this model some real substance for vintage-watch fans. The hand-wound version is particularly appealing.

The Tissot PRX Chronograph Automatic features a 42mm stainless-steel case with the collection’s signature angular profile and an integrated steel bracelet. Its dial uses a contrasting three-register layout, with chronograph counters at three, six, and nine o’clock, and a date display. Powered by Tissot’s automatic Valjoux A05.H31 movement, the watch offers a 60-hour power reserve. A scratch-resistant sapphire crystal protects the dial, and the case is water-resistant to 100 meters.

The PRX has become one of the more recognizable modern Swiss sports-watch designs, and the chronograph adds a layer of mechanical interest to its integrated-bracelet format. For someone building a collection, it offers a taste of the Seventies sports-watch aesthetic without the price tag attached to many of its luxury counterparts.

The Timex Q Continental Chronograph features a 36mm stainless-steel case with brushed surfaces, polished edges, and an integrated stainless-steel bracelet. Its textured dial features contrasting chronograph subdials, luminous hands and hour markers, and a fixed tachymeter bezel for calculating average speed. Powered by a quartz chronograph movement, it includes a stopwatch function and 24-hour display. A mineral crystal protects the dial, while 50-meter water resistance makes it suitable for everyday wear.

Its compact proportions and distinctly retro styling make it an appealing entry point for collectors interested in the smaller, more experimental sports watches of the Seventies and Eighties.

The Bulova 150th Anniversary Shelby Racer Chronograph features a 43mm stainless-steel bullhead case inspired by the 1967 Shelby Ford Mustang GT500. Its blue and white color scheme carries across the dial and rubber strap, while a black tachymeter ring, 12 o’clock crown and pushers, and Shelby Cobra branding reinforce its racing theme. Powered by Bulova’s Precisionist quartz movement, the chronograph can measure elapsed time to one-thousandth of a second. An antireflective sapphire crystal protects the dial, and the watch is water-resistant to 50 meters. The limited edition was produced in a run of 7500 pieces and originally included a miniature GT500 model. Its unusual bullhead layout and direct connection to American muscle-car history make it an interesting crossover piece for collectors who enjoy watches as much for their automotive associations as their movements.

The Junghans Form C Chronoscope features a 40mm stainless-steel case measuring 10.5mm thick, with a clean, minimalist dial and a slim profile. Its matte-finished dial features luminous hands, a small seconds subdial, a date display, and two chronograph counters for measuring elapsed minutes and hours. Powered by a quartz movement, the watch offers straightforward timekeeping without the maintenance demands of a mechanical chronograph. A scratch-resistant sapphire crystal protects the dial, while 50-meter water resistance makes it suitable for everyday use.

Junghans has a long association with German design, particularly the restrained Bauhaus-influenced aesthetic, and the Form C is a good example of that philosophy. It makes a compelling choice for someone who appreciates thoughtful industrial design and prefers a chronograph that doesn’t rely on oversize cases or racing-inspired graphics.

This Patek Philippe Perpetual Calendar Chronograph is considered a “Grand Complication,” the absolute peak of watchmaking produced by Patek, one of watchmaking’s most prestigious and important manufacturers. This watch features a rose-gold case, but the real draw here is the movement. The self-winding caliber CHR 29-535 PS Q movement is visible through a sapphire-crystal caseback, and on the dial side of the watch, you’ll spot rattrapante chronograph hands displayed alongside perpetual calendar and moon-phase displays. The 5205 is truly a masterpiece of high horology, combining ultimate functionality with elegant design and surpassing craftsmanship. Note: This is a pre-owned watch.

The Portugieser is a classic chrono with a clean, elegant design. It has a round stainless-steel case, measuring 41mm in diameter and 13mm in thickness. The dial features two subdials at the six and 12 o’clock positions. It runs on IWC-manufactured caliber 69355 automatic movement with a power reserve of approximately 46 hours, visible through a sapphire-crystal caseback. The watch comes with either a leather or stainless-steel strap, is water-resistant up to 30 meters, and is a popular choice among watch enthusiasts and collectors. Note: This is a pre-owned watch.

The Tissot PRS 516 features a stainless-steel case with a sporty dial, luminous hands and hour markers, and a fixed tachymeter bezel. The automatic version uses Tissot’s own A05.H31 movement, with a power reserve of approximately 60 hours. Its chronograph function includes a central seconds hand and a 30-minute counter, alongside a date display. A scratch-resistant sapphire-crystal and transparent caseback showcase the watch’s construction.

The collection’s roots in motorsport-inspired design date back to the Sixties, giving it a bit of history beyond the usual modern sports-watch formula. The automatic version is especially appealing to collectors who want a traditional Swiss mechanical chronograph with a more overt racing influence.

The limited-edition Chopard Mille Miglia GT XL embodies the excitement of the historic Mille Miglia race. It features a sturdy stainless-steel case, automatic chronograph movement, and a white dial with easy-to-read numerals and indices. The watch’s functions include hour, minute, and seconds hands, a date window with a magnification loupe, and subdials that track the elapsed minutes and hours of the chronograph, plus a continuously running seconds hand. This Swiss-made watch features a 48-hour power reserve and a 44mm case diameter. This watch is limited to just 1000 pieces.

The Prospex Speedtimer is a solar-powered, precision timepiece inspired by the classic chronograph designs of the Sixties. Featuring a Seiko V192 movement with a six-month power reserve, it boasts a black dial, a tachymeter bezel, LumiBrite hands and markers, a curved sapphire crystal, a date calendar, stainless-steel construction, and 100-meter water resistance.

The Navitimer was initially designed for aviation professionals and enthusiasts, a portmanteau of “navigation” and “time.” This take on the classic Navitimer features a slide-rule bezel to complete basic calculations, a self-winding automatic movement, and a chronograph function, plus three subdials. It comes in a stainless-steel or 18k-gold case, with luminous markers and a date-display window on the dial. The watch is water-resistant to 30 meters and has a power reserve of up to 70 hours, making it a reliable and functional watch for everyday wear. Note: This is a pre-owned watch.

The TAG Heuer Formula 1 Chronograph features a 43mm stainless-steel case with a fixed tachymeter bezel and a sporty blue dial with luminous hands and applied hour markers. Its quartz chronograph movement measures elapsed time in tenths of a second and includes a 30-minute counter and date display. A scratch-resistant sapphire crystal protects the dial, while the screw-down crown and 200-meter water resistance give the watch added durability. Depending on the reference, the bezel may use ceramic or coated steel, and the watch is available with different dial and bracelet configurations.

TAG Heuer’s motorsport history makes the Formula 1 line a natural fit for automotive enthusiasts, and its connection to the brand’s racing partnerships gives it an identity beyond its stopwatch functionality. It’s also an approachable way into one of the most recognizable names in Swiss sports watches.

The primary distinction between a regular watch and a chronograph lies in a chronograph’s stopwatch functions. A chronograph enables its users to measure the elapsed time of an event, like one lap of a racetrack or how long you’ve had your steaks on the grill. All the while, your watch is keeping track of the current time.

In addition to basic timekeeping and stopwatch capabilities, many chronograph watches come equipped with a tachymeter, a scale used to measure speed based on elapsed time over a specific distance (usually one mile), and a telemeter, which measures distance based on the speed of sound and elapsed time. Water resistance is another common feature, protecting the watch from damage due to moisture or immersion in water.

Chronographs come in various types, each with its own characteristics:

A chronograph combines the functionality of a traditional watch with a built-in stopwatch. This allows users to measure elapsed time and split times, which makes it ideal for driving.

To use the stopwatch functions on a chronograph timepiece, you press the corresponding pushers (button) on the side of the watch to start, stop, and reset the stopwatch. Certain chronograph watches may have additional pushers for more advanced functions like split or lap times. Due to the extra mechanical complexity required, watches with more pushers will typically cost more than monopusher (single-pusher) timepieces.

A tachymeter is a scale on the bezel or dial of certain chronograph watches. Its purpose is to measure the speed of an object using the watch’s built-in stopwatch, based on the time passed. To use the tachymeter, start the chronograph function when something starts (like a car crossing a start line) and stop it when it’s finished (when the car hits the finish line). The tachymeter scale will then display the car’s average speed, based on the time it took to get from A to B.

Proper maintenance of your chronograph depends on its type. Mechanical chronograph watches require regular servicing (roughly every 5–7 years) to ensure optimal performance. Quartz chronograph watches may need battery replacements, and solar-powered watches should be exposed to light regularly to maintain their charge. Be sure to always follow the manufacturer’s maintenance guidelines.

#4588. A bull and a male donkey’s sexual relationship turns heads

Published Nov 2, 2026 11:00 AM EST

Sex between two animals of the same sex is widespread. Over 1,000 animal species from nematode worms to penguins to cattle all dabble in same-sex interactions. But a relationship between a bull named Achille and a male donkey named Patrocolo is raising eyebrows. The pair lives on a plateau in Ethiopia, and both could have chosen partners of the opposite sex and same species on numerous occasions. However, they continued to choose each other, despite belonging to different owners and only seeing one another when spending time in a pasture. A study published today in the journal Current Biology chronicles this surprising union.

“The sexual interactions between Achille, the bull, and Patroclo, the male donkey, were not isolated events,” Elisabetta Palagi, a study co-author and evolutionary biologist at the Università di Pisa (UNIPI) in Italy, said in a statement. “What really caught our attention was that these interactions were embedded in a very selective and consistent social relationship between the two individuals.”

The team first spotted these interactions while conducting another study earlier this year. They saw Achille mounting Patroclo, and were surprised to see that Patroclo did not try to avoid the bull, kick him, or show any defensive reactions.

“They repeatedly chose to stay close to each other and engaged in many different affiliative behaviors, such as licking, rubbing, and nuzzling, alongside the repeated mounting behavior,” added co-author André da Cruz, a PhD student at UNIPI. “Importantly, this was happening in a social environment where both animals had access to other potential partners, including individuals of both sexes and of their own species.”

The team recorded all of the interactions they witnessed involving either Achille or Patroclo. In total, the observed 51 mountings between the male bull and donkey from March 6 to March 19. In these interactions, Patroclo often presented his hindquarters to Achille and then nipped at the bull. They repeatedly directed most of their sexual and social interactions toward each other, and the team reported no indication from the bull or donkey that either wished to discourage those advances. Achille mounted another male donkey only twice, and that other male showed avoidance behaviors and threatening expressions, like flattened ears.

“We believe the key finding is not simply that a bull mounted a male donkey,” said study co-author Martina Francesconi, also a PhD student at UNIPI. “It is that this unusual sexual behavior was part of a broader, selective social relationship. Our observations suggest that it cannot be easily explained simply by a lack of alternative mating opportunities, although we cannot say from this study exactly what function these sexual interactions may have had.”

According to the team, these observations have wider implications for our understanding of how sexual behavior is a complex social trait that goes beyond its role in reproduction. It also raises important questions for future studies, including if these interactions are primarily related to social bonding, what the benefits are, and if they play a role in reducing tension or maintaining relationships. In previous studies, same-sex mounting in nonhuman primates appears to be a form of conflict resolution and way to strengthen bonds, and may help male macaques reproduce more successfully.

“More broadly, we would like to better understand how social relationships shape sexual behavior and how behavioral flexibility allows animals to navigate complex social environments,” said Palagi. “We see this study as a starting point for asking these broader questions.”

#4587. Cops Offer Sage Advice to Porsche 911 GT3 Driver Who Wants His Car Back After Police Chase

The 21-year-old Porsche driver was reduced to tears after his escape attempt ended with him in handcuffs and his car headed for the impound lot.

Having access to a Porsche 911 GT3 at 21 years old is one thing. Having the maturity to drive it responsibly on public roads is another. A young driver in Washington recently discovered that lacking the latter can have serious consequences—like ending up in the back of a police car in tears, facing the possibility of losing a very expensive sports car.

According to the Snohomish County Sheriff's Office, the incident began on October 18, 2026. Shortly before 6:30 p.m., Sergeant Wallin spotted the blue Porsche allegedly being driven recklessly on northbound Interstate 5. The officer initiated a pursuit, but quickly called it off when police say the driver drove through downtown Everett at high speed.

However, a brightly colored Porsche is not exactly discreet, especially one that appears to be a 991.2-generation GT3 modified with a 911 GT3 RS hood and rear spoiler. Police deputies and drone operators were able to keep track of the car which allegedly continued to drive recklessly. Eventually, police were able to get ahead of the Porsche, and successfully deployed spike strips.

The chase was over, but not the drama. Audio from police bodycam footage reveals that the Porsche driver was crying while being read his Miranda rights and arrested. Then things turned worse for the driver when the police informed him that his car was likely going to end up belonging to the sheriff’s office.

"Is there anything I can do to get my car back?" the driver asked. “Not run from the police,” is the officer’s quick (and wise) response.

The sheriff's office is now pursuing the legal seizure of the Porsche, meaning the driver could potentially lose his GT3 permanently. This could end up being a very expensive lesson for the young man. If you want to drive a Porsche like a race car, you should probably take it to a racetrack.

#4586. Aloe found in ancient Egyptian mummy skull

Published Nov 2, 2026 12:58 PM EST

Archaeologists have identified a previously undocumented ingredient used in ancient Egyptian mummifications—and a famous medieval medicine concocted from the mummies themselves. At Germany’s Marburg University, researchers pinpointed traces of aloe-associated plant material in a 2,700-year-old mummy skull, and a popular centuries’ old apothecary cure-all known as Mumia vera aegyptiaca.

There is no one way to make a mummy. Mummification methods have varied across the world for thousands of years, even within a single culture. Ancient Egyptians honed their own processes over generations, and archaeologists are still sifting through millennia’s worth of artifacts and texts to better understand the iconic postmortem procedures.

Egyptology first truly took off in Europe during the late 18th century, but people’s fascination with mummies goes much further back in time. However, the long and complex medicinal history of mummy-derived treatments collectively called Mumia likely began as a 12th century mistranslation. Persian pharmacists often used a black pitch called mumiya in wound care, which medieval translators of Latin later mistook for similarly dark materials used in Egyptian mummification. This eventually led to an entire trade network centered on the import of powdered mummy remains sold by apothecaries as a Mumia cure-all—and sometimes even an aphrodisiac—for centuries.

Archaeologists have already documented many mummification ingredients derived from various minerals, animals, and plants. These span a range of coniferous tars and reins, oils, fats, beeswax, and bitumen, as well as rarer regional plant distillations like dammar and elemi. Knowing there is still much more to learn, the team at Marburg University recently analyzed 24 historically related objects stored at various institutions. These included an Egyptian mummified skull dated to the 8th century BCE, as well as an 18th century historical preparation of Mumia housed at Heidelberg Pharmacy Museum.

Their findings were recently published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, and offer the first molecular evidence of mummy-related materials directly derived from aloe. This is particularly important, since “aloe” often historically referred to a variety of plants like agarwood outside the Aloe genus. According to Tanja Pommerening, a study co-author and director of Marburg University’s Institute for the History of Pharmacy and Medicine, the detection of aloe in Mumia is also particularly significant. Prior to this study, many researchers assumed medieval authors drew their Mumia recipes from biblical passages. These include John 19:39, which references a “mixture of myrrh and aloes.”

“The new findings suggest that this association may have deeper historical roots,” explained Pommerening.

However, since only two of the 24 artifacts in the study yielded traces of aloe, the frequency of the plant’s use in mummification and Mumia remains unclear. It’s possible that preparers may have only incorporated the material during certain historical periods, or depending on its availability. Still, Pommerening and her colleagues plan to continue similar examinations of other historical objects.

“Our goal is not only to analyze the chemical composition of ancient medicines and embalming materials, but also to gain a deeper understanding of their production, use, historical transmission, and cultural context,” added study co-author and Marburg University biologist Raphael Reher.

#4585. Harley-Davidson’s electric motorcycle brand LiveWire warns it may not survive

Harley-Davidson-born electric motorcycle maker LiveWire has issued a troubling warning about its financial future, announcing that it has substantial doubt about its ability to continue operating as a going concern. The news sent LiveWire’s stock plunging more than 40% on Thursday morning as the company withdrew its full-year financial guidance.

The announcement comes despite some signs of improving sales, with LiveWire reporting a 38% increase in third-quarter revenue to $7.9 million and a 21% rise in motorcycle unit sales. However, the company continues to burn through cash, reporting a net loss of $18.6 million for the quarter.

LiveWire’s cash reserves have also dwindled significantly, falling from $82.8 million at the end of 2025 to just $39.9 million as of September 30, 2026.

The company has now formed a special restructuring committee to explore potential financing arrangements, strategic partnerships, investments, or even a sale. It also withdrew its previous guidance projecting a $70 million to $80 million operating loss for 2026.

The financial warning comes at a particularly pivotal moment for LiveWire, which is preparing to launch its most affordable electric motorcycles yet.

The upcoming LiveWire S4 Honcho series represents a major departure from the company’s existing premium electric motorcycles, offering smaller, lighter, and significantly more affordable models designed to attract a much broader audience of riders with a starting price below US $5,000.

The lower prices could dramatically increase LiveWire’s sales volumes, especially as the company attempts to move beyond the relatively small market for high-dollar electric motorcycles. The Honcho lineup is also expected to help lower the barrier to entry for new riders, with approachable electric motorcycles that eliminate the complexity of clutch and gear shifting.

LiveWire is also preparing to showcase its latest developments at EICMA in Milan next week, where it is expected to display new models and further expand its upcoming electric motorcycle lineup.

Whether those new motorcycles can arrive quickly enough to turn around the company’s financial situation remains to be seen.

This is genuinely sad news to see. If there’s any legacy motorcycle manufacturer that deserves to succeed in the electric motorcycle space, it’s Harley-Davidson.

Make all the jokes you want about old dudes in leather jackets riding around on loud, chrome-covered motorcycles. But the fact is that Harley-Davidson was taking electric motorcycles seriously when most other major motorcycle manufacturers were still pretending they didn’t exist.

Harley-Davidson didn’t just dip its toes into electric motorcycles. It dove in headfirst, developing the original LiveWire electric motorcycle well over a decade ago and eventually bringing a highly acclaimed production bike to market in 2019. That’s right, Harley-Davidson had a legitimately impressive electric motorcycle on the road before COVID was even a thing. Meanwhile, most of its legacy competitors are only now starting to roll out their first serious electric offerings.

Maybe it's news to Electrek, but while Harley was contemplating electric motorcycles, Zero was selling them for over a decade and continues to do so. There are some high end bikes that Livewire just didn't compete with yet cost $30k when it first came out damaging the brand perception. Newer, lower priced models don't help.

There is also competition from run around eScooters that are way cheaper even cheaper than upcoming Honcho.

And that’s what makes this so frustrating. Harley-Davidson did the hard part. It invested early, developed excellent technology, received rave reviews, and proved that electric motorcycles could be thrilling, premium machines. But building great motorcycles and building a profitable electric motorcycle business have turned out to be two very different challenges.

The timing is especially unfortunate because I genuinely believe LiveWire’s upcoming S4 Honcho series could be exactly what the company needs. These smaller, significantly more affordable electric motorcycles could finally open LiveWire up to a younger audience that doesn’t have $15,000 to drop on a flagship motorcycle but still wants something fun, stylish, and electric for $5,000.

In many ways, that audience seems like a much more natural fit for LiveWire’s branding and ethos than the premium motorcycle market it has been chasing for years.

I really hope LiveWire can find what it needs to get through this difficult period. After spending more than a decade helping drag the legacy motorcycle industry kicking and screaming into the electric age, it would be a real shame to see the company stumble just as its most promising chapter might be about to begin.

#4584. Dinosaur blood found in fossils for the first time

Published Nov 2, 2026 3:00 PM EST

Paleontologists regularly discover fossilized dinosaur bones, but they sometimes locate footprints and prehistoric shells. On rare occasions, researchers have even identified the ancient indentations of a dinosaur’s skin or feathers. But fossilized cells? Researchers have long assumed such microscopic levels of preservation were impossible. But, once again, nature has proven otherwise.

In a study published today in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), an international team of paleontologists confirmed the presence of intact biomolecules and mineralized red blood cells inside fossils of a 115-million-year-old dinosaur. Although previous work has suggested similar possibilities, the team’s research is the first to chemically identify oxygen-carrying blood compounds known as heme.

“This really is a landmark discovery,” Kliti Grice, a study co-author and chemist at Curtin University in Australia, said in a statement. “These findings challenge longstanding assumptions that certain biomolecules such as hemoglobin cannot survive deep time.”

The evidence exists inside the fossilized limb bones of a juvenile Aratasaurus museunacionali. Discovered in 2008, A. museunacionali was an Early Cretaceous theropod that lived in present-day northeastern Brazil. The fossils suggest a dinosaur measuring over 10 feet long and weighing about 75 pounds, but given its young age, A. museunacionali likely grew even larger.

After carefully examining thin slices of the fossils, paleontologists located the mineralized red blood cell molecular components, along with a complex manganese oxide called hausmannite. This material helped maintain the cellular structures of heme, a ring-shaped molecule that contains iron and binds many proteins, especially hemoglobin. The hausmannite also helped preserve additional biomolecules found in the blood, such as the amino acids in collagen. The study’s authors theorize this level of preservation could only occur following a rapid burial in an environment that was rich in microbes, but low in oxygen at the same time.

Grice and her collaborators said that their discovery has wider implications for molecular-level paleontology. Further study could help advance our understanding of blood’s evolution, dinosaur metabolism, and ancient animals’ activity levels. The knowledge that this type of preservation is possible at all could even extend far beyond Earth. If such delicate biomolecules fossilize over millions of years in harsh environments, then it’s possible similar traces of life may linger elsewhere in the universe.

#4583. Jasion Poki review: The Electric Minibike that packs heavy-duty fun

In our transportation reporting, we rarely come across something as fun as today’s review of the Jasion Poki.

The Poki is a severely overpowered electric minibike that looks like it came from yesteryear. If the power isn’t enough, it also packs some cool tricks, and we’re not (just) talking about wheelies this time.

So taking a look at this bad boy, it just screams fun. It is really low to the ground, has a big, wide seat large enough for 2 people as long as they are under 350lbs total, and has pegs for 2 people and a basket, great for carrying a picnic and an extra helmet.

This thing is built like a tank, and it tips the scales accordingly. Getting this thing in my SUV ruptured a few discs in my back, though its compact nature means it fit quite well. Loosen the handlebars and it is downright compact. But that weight is strangely like 50lbs heavier than I would expect at close to 140lbs.

That also makes the built-in wheelies a little bit more suspect. My son, who is by now becoming an expert at wheelies, found this one to be a bit more difficult than the auto wheelies on bikes like the Anyland or new Yozma IN11.

OK so not only does this little powerhouse get you (and your friend) around town in style and it also makes wheelies a bit easier; but it also has a huge Bluetooth speaker in the back that sounds like a Harley and is all synced up with the actual controller so it sounds real.

Sure, it is a gimmick, but it is a fun one, and it might actually make the low-down bike a little safer since it is going to be out of the sight of most cars.

I love this thing. It is my favorite bike to go to the beach on (and it does well in the sand with those fat tires). But I think there are some big misses here. First of all, it has no business going over 40mph. Not only does it feel scary with those tiny wheels, but speed wobbles puts both the rider a possible second rider at significant risk here. This is a fun bike and it should top out at 20-28mph max. Keep all the torque, just cut out the power at a reasonable top speed.

Also it should weigh a lot less. At 140lbs, it is silly hard to get into the back of a car, which it easily fits in. Making the frame aluminum would go a long way here. Also, if this thing rolled on top of you, it would be a bad day.

Make this thing safer and more portable, and I’d recommend everyone with a beach commute to get one. As it stands, best for responsible adults with strong backs and a Peter Pan complex.

The Poki is currently priced at $1,799, and customers can get 5% off with the code Electrek.

#4582. President Trump Reportedly Promised Audi Tariff Relief for Building Georgia Factory

The German automaker is betting big on the United States, and the Trump Administration seemingly wants to reward them.

President Donald Trump announced Audi’s plan to build its first-ever United States production facility in Macon, Georgia, on Saturday, October 24. And now the commander-in-chief is reportedly prepared to offer the German automaker tariff relief as a result.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that the Trump administration has promised to ease tariffs on automakers that commit to U.S. manufacturing, and Audi may be the first to reap the benefit. Audi executives received assurances from the administration that the Commerce Department would soon institute a tariff-relief program for companies that invest in domestic production, according to people familiar with the plan. The automaker is set to invest $4 billion in a production facility that will build 200,000 vehicles annually by the early 2030s.

The details of the tariff relief plan have yet to be announced. However, the WSJ reported that the plan will likely allow automakers that invest in U.S. factories to receive exemptions or offsets for tariffs on imported vehicles or parts. Automakers would need to start factory construction before the end of next year to qualify, a person familiar with the plan said to the WSJ. Two sources briefed on the matter who spoke to Reuters said Audi pushed the U.S. to ⁠cut the current 15 percent tariffs to 7.5 percent, but that Commerce Department officials were expected to agree to a final rate around 10 percent.

Similarly, the automotive tariff relief plan will likely share origins with a Commerce Department program established for tariffs on polysilicon, according to the WSJ. Under that program, solar companies can submit plans to move production to the Commerce Department and receive approval for tariff exemptions for certain products. Audi would benefit greatly from such a tariff relief program; it currently imports all of its models to the U.S. market from Mexico or Europe, and paid $1.4 billion in duties last year. The Volkswagen Group as a whole paid $4 billion in U.S. tariffs in 2025.

“We are not able to provide further comment at this stage,” an Audi spokesperson told Road & Track when asked for more information about the report.

Audi chief executive officer Gernot Doellner joined Trump on stage at a campaign rally on Sunday, October 25, where the president announced the new factory. Doellner said Audi’s new plant will create around 4500 jobs. The German automaker has also committed to building an additional 25,000 Audi units each year in South Carolina. Audi’s high-end Q7, Q8, and Q9 SUVs are slated for production at its future U.S. facilities.

"This decision was preceded by many months of careful planning and intense negotiations," Doellner said. "If the American president invites you, you accept the invitation. That is what respect for the office and for the country in which we invest demands."

Volkswagen’s Supervisory Board, which includes worker and labor-union representatives, still needs to sign off on Audi’s Georgia factory before any of these plans go forward. The board will meet in the coming weeks to finalize the plan, a plan that Audi executives are probably crossing their fingers over. The luxury automaker’s North American sales fell 16 percent in 2025, amid sticker price increases and a temporary pause on new vehicle deliveries.

A New York transplant hailing from the Pacific Northwest, Emmet White has a passion for anything that goes: cars, bicycles, planes, and motorcycles. After learning to ride at 17, Emmet worked in the motorcycle industry before joining Autoweek in 2022 and Road & Track in 2024. The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

#4581. Watchful mama bear Gemini wins 2026 Helicopter Mom Award

Published Nov 2, 2026 4:07 PM EST

Even bears can be helicopter parents. The term coined in the 1990s by child development researchers Foster Cline and Jim Fay describes overly cautious parents who constantly monitor, control, and hover over (like a helicopter) their children’s activities out of fear.

For these watchful tendencies, the U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska has awarded a brown bear (Ursus arctos) named Gemini with the 2026 Helicopter Mom Award.

“We understand her choice, weighing the dangers of being around other bears at a prime fishing location,” the rangers write. “Still, we hope we see a lot more of them next year.”

The numbers also back up Gemini and other mother bears’ watchfulness. Brown bear cubs in Alaska have a roughly 50 percent survival rate within their first year, while the black bear (Ursus americanus) cub survival rate can range from 51 to 88 percent depending on the location. Gemini has also had cubs in 2023 and 2024.

The Rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of Southeast Alaska, including the capital city of Juneau. The vast area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears. Like their beefy counterparts further north in Katmai National Park, the bears return annually each summer to eat salmon and teach their young how to fish and survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here exhibits their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.
